title: AI and You
text:
🧭 About the Class
AI is everywhere now. It writes, draws, talks, answers questions, and even pretends to be a friend. Some people say it thinks like a human brain. Others say it only looks that way. In this class, you decide.
We’ll see what AI can do, learn the story of how it was built, look at how it works (including the idea it copied from brain cells), and try it out for real tasks. By the end, you’ll know how to use AI well, spot it when it’s wrong, and decide for yourself what you think about it and the world it’s building.

Unit 1: Where AI Came From
The story of AI, from Alan Turing’s question “Can machines think?” to ChatGPT. You play the imitation game and act out the Klingon Room. You play against a game bot made of rules. You label pictures the way the ImageNet workers did. The class builds a timeline on the wall. You also write your first answer to the Big Question.


Unit 2: Brains and Neural Networks
How simple rules make complex behavior, how brain cells work, and how computer scientists copied the idea. You become a neuron, then the class trains a neural network made of people, using cards for made-up creatures. You build and train a real AI on a computer. You train your own AI with a camera. You see how AI sees pictures and how chatbots write.


Unit 3: Using AI Well
The heart of the class. You learn to write good prompts and ask follow-up questions. You get feedback on your own writing. You check facts, test translations in your home language, check AI’s math, and write prompts for pictures. Then you finish a real project that uses AI to solve a problem in your life. You share it with the class.


Unit 4: When AI Gets It Wrong
AI makes things up. It can be unfair to some people. It can be used to fake pictures and voices. You catch a chatbot inventing facts about our school. You act out the story of Clever Hans the horse. You test your eyes against fake faces. And you find out why AI cheat detectors blame students who are learning English.


Unit 5: AI in the Real World
What AI means for your privacy, your future job, and the news you see. You find the hidden location inside a photo. You sort real messages from scams. You break your dream job into tasks. And you watch a news feed learn what you like.


Unit 6: AI and Our Future
AI art, AI friends, the hidden costs of AI, the rules for AI, and possible futures. You act out the trolley problem and the paper clip machine. In the last lesson, you replace a “brain” one cell at a time. Then you read your answer from the first day, and answer the Big Question again.

title: 1.1 - What Is AI?
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Your phone opens when it sees your face. A video app knows what you want to watch next. A chatbot writes a story in two seconds.
All of these use AI. But what is AI? How is it different from a normal computer program? And is it like a human brain?
Today you sort things into AI and not AI. You try to teach a computer what a cat is. Then you play a drawing game against an AI.
Look at these 10 things. Which ones use AI?
Press a choice on each card: AI, Not AI, or Not sure. Talk with a partner. You don’t need to agree.

title: 1.1 - What Is AI?
text:
👀 Show the answers

They all learn from examples, and they all make guesses.
The calculator and the alarm clock don’t learn. They only follow rules that a person wrote.

title: 1.1 - What Is AI?
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.1.1 - What Does “AI” Mean?
AI means artificial intelligence. Artificial means made by people. Intelligence means the ability to learn, understand, and solve problems.
So AI is a computer program that does things that usually need human thinking. AI can see faces, understand speech, translate languages, and write. Most AI today does these things in a new way. It learns from examples. Let’s see why.



1.1.2 - Can You Write a Rule for “Cat”?
A normal computer program follows rules. A person writes every rule.



Program
A rule a person wrote




🔢 Calculator
If someone presses 2 + 3 =, show 5.


⏰ Alarm clock
If the time is 7:00, ring.



These rules are easy to write. Now try a hard one.

A computer gets a picture. Write a rule that tells the computer: Is this a cat?
Start like this: “It is a cat if it has …”
Write your rule on your sheet. Then test your rule on these three pictures. Does your rule give the right answer for each one?







Probably not. Many students write: “It is a cat if it has pointy ears, whiskers, and four legs.”

Picture B is a fox. It has pointy ears, whiskers, and four legs. The rule says “cat.” That’s wrong.
Picture C is a cat. It’s sleeping, so you can’t see its legs. The rule says “not a cat.” That’s wrong too.

You can fix the rule. But then a new picture breaks it again.

So scientists tried a different idea:

Don’t write the rules.
Show the computer many examples. Each example has the right answer.
Let the computer find the pattern by itself.

This idea is called machine learning. The examples are called data.







Normal program: a person writes the rules. The computer follows them.
Machine learning: a person gives examples. The computer makes its own rules.
After it learns, it works like a normal program. The difference is who made the rules.

title: 1.1 - What Is AI?
text:
🛠️ Try It

1.1.3 - Quick, Draw!
Quick, Draw! is a game made by Google. You draw. An AI tries to guess what you’re drawing.
The AI learned from about 50 million drawings. People from all over the world made them.
✏️ Open Quick, Draw!


Click Let’s Draw!
The game shows a word. Draw it. You have 20 seconds. (If you don’t know the word, ask a partner.)
Play all 6 rounds.
Write your results on your sheet. Did the AI guess? About how many seconds did it take?



The game saves your drawings and your country. Google shares the drawings with scientists around the world. Don’t write your name or anything private in a drawing.


The AI learned from millions of drawings. Your first lines looked like the start of drawings it saw before. So it made a prediction: a best guess. It didn’t wait for the whole picture.

title: 1.2 - Can a Machine Think?
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In 1950, a scientist named Alan Turing asked a big question: Can a machine think?
People don’t agree on what “think” means. So Turing asked a new question that you can test: Can a machine talk so well that you can’t tell it’s a machine?
He made a game to find out. Today, you play his game with a real AI.
Is it thinking? Mark each one on your sheet: Yes, No, or Not sure.
Compare with a partner.

title: 1.2 - Can a Machine Think?
text:
🔢
A calculator adds 375 + 498.


🐕
A dog finds its way home.


🔓
A phone opens when it sees your face.


🧩
You solve a puzzle.


🌻
A plant turns toward the sun.


💬
A chatbot writes a poem.





Probably not. People don’t agree on what “thinking” means. Scientists still argue about it today.
Alan Turing saw this problem in 1950. So he didn’t try to define “thinking.” He made a test instead.

title: 1.2 - Can a Machine Think?
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.2.1 - The Imitation Game
Turing called his test the imitation game. (To imitate means to copy someone.) Today, people call it the Turing test.






A judge sends questions to two hidden players, A and B.
One player is a person. One player is a machine.
The judge can’t see or hear them. The judge only reads their typed answers.
The judge decides: Which one is the machine?

If the judge can’t tell, the machine passes the test.



1.2.2 - Has a Machine Passed?
In 2025, scientists played Turing’s game with almost 300 judges. Each judge chatted with a person and a chatbot for 5 minutes. Then the judge picked: Which one is the human?





GPT-4.5 was picked as the human 73% of the time. The judges picked the chatbot more often than the real person. The researchers said it passed Turing’s test. But it only did this well with a persona. The scientists told it: Act like a shy young person who uses slang. Short answers with small mistakes look human. (ELIZA is a chatbot from 1966. You meet it in the next lesson.)

title: 1.3 - The First Chatbot
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In 1966, people at a university in Massachusetts talked to a computer program named ELIZA. ELIZA acted like a counselor. Some people told it their secrets. Some people believed it understood them.
ELIZA understood nothing. It followed a list of rules that one person wrote.
Today, you play ELIZA yourself and see how it works. Then you act out a famous puzzle: a person who answers notes in a language they don’t know.
Work with a partner (or a group of 3, taking turns). One of you is ELIZA. ELIZA can only answer with the rule card. ELIZA can’t think of anything new!

Being ELIZA is easy. You don’t need to understand anything. You only look for the key words and follow the card.
Sometimes ELIZA’s answer sounds caring. Sometimes it sounds strange. ELIZA can’t tell the difference.

title: 1.3 - The First Chatbot
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.3.1 - How ELIZA Works
ELIZA was made in 1966 by Joseph Weizenbaum, a professor at MIT. ELIZA doesn’t learn. Weizenbaum wrote every rule by hand. Here is how ELIZA answers one sentence:







ELIZA looks for key words. It doesn’t know what the words mean.
If no rule matches, ELIZA says something that fits anything, like “Please go on.”
ELIZA is a normal program: a person wrote the rules (like the calculator in Lesson 1.1).


Here is a real conversation with ELIZA. Find one answer where ELIZA copied your words and swapped “my” for “your.”



A conversation with a copy of ELIZA made in 2005. The person’s words come from Weizenbaum’s 1966 paper about ELIZA. (Screenshot, public domain, Wikimedia Commons)





1.3.2 - People Believed It
Weizenbaum’s secretary knew that ELIZA was only a program. She watched him build it. But one day, she was chatting with ELIZA. She asked Weizenbaum to leave the room so she could talk to it alone.
Many people felt that ELIZA understood them. Today, we call this the ELIZA effect.

title: 1.3 - The First Chatbot
text:
🛠️ Try It

1.3.3 - The Chinese Room

A philosopher named John Searle asked people to imagine this:

A person sits in a closed room. They do not know the language of the notes.
Notes come in through a slot.
The person has a rule book. It says: “If you see these shapes, send back those shapes.”
The person finds the shapes and copies the reply. They pass it out.
Outside, people who know the language read the replies. The replies make sense! They think someone in the room knows the language.

Does anyone in the room understand the language?

Act it out: the Klingon Room. Searle imagined notes in Chinese, a language he couldn’t read. We’ll use Klingon. It’s a language made up for the Star Trek TV shows and movies. (Some fans really speak it!)





Work in a group of 2 to 4: one person in the room, the rest outside. Each group needs one rule book and one set of note cards. (Only 4 in class? Be one group, and take turns going in the room.)


One person is in the room. Sit behind a folder or a book so the others can’t see you. Take the rule book.
Everyone else is outside. Share the note cards. Fold back the English part.
Pass one note into the room. The person in the room finds the note that looks exactly the same in the rule book. They copy the reply on the back. Pass it out.
Outside: check the reply with the English on your card. Does it make sense?
Pass in at least 6 notes. Then switch: a new person goes in the room.



The room answered: “Yes. I am learning Klingon.”
But the person in the room doesn’t know any Klingon. The answer sounds right, and it is not true.
Now look at the note about the bathroom. The room said: “I don’t understand.” That one is true! But the room only said it because a rule told it to.


Look at three notes: bIpIv'a'?, bIghung'a'? and bIQuch'a'?. Each reply sends the same word back, but bI becomes jI: jIpIv, jIghung, jIQuch.
In Klingon, bI means “you” and jI means “I.” It’s the same swap ELIZA makes, when “my” becomes “your.”
If you were in the room, maybe you started to guess replies without the book. You found a pattern. Did you understand any more Klingon?

Searle said: the person in the room doesn’t understand the language. They only follow rules. A computer is the same. It follows rules, so it doesn’t understand anything.
Other people disagree. They say: maybe the person doesn’t understand, but the whole room (the person plus the book) does.
What do you think?

title: 1.4 - Rules Win at Games
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In 1958, a newspaper wrote about a new computer. It said the computer would soon “walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence.”
Did that happen? Not in 1958. Not for a long time.
For about 40 years, scientists tried to build AI out of rules. Rules didn’t work for seeing or talking. But rules did work for one thing: games. Today, you play a game against a bot made only of rules. Then you break it.
Long ago, people made big promises about AI. Read each one. Did it come true by the time they said? Mark your sheet.

title: 1.4 - Rules Win at Games
text:
Year
Who said it
The promise




A
1958

B
1958

C
1970

None of them came true by the time they said.
Parts of Promise A came true much later. Today, AI can talk, see, and write. Can it know that it exists? Nobody knows.
Promise B came true later. A computer beat the world chess champion in 1997. That’s 39 years later, not 10.
Promise C didn’t come true by the 1970s. Today, some people say AI is getting close. Other people strongly disagree. You’ll think about this in Unit 6.

title: 1.4 - Rules Win at Games
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.4.1 - AI Winters
In 1956, scientists met at Dartmouth College. They gave the new field a name: artificial intelligence. They thought smart machines were only a few years away. Governments and companies gave them a lot of money.
Progress was much slower than the promises. So the money stopped. This happened two times.
People call these times AI winters. (In winter, plants stop growing. In an AI winter, AI research stopped growing.)






The promises in the Warm Up were hype. In 1958 and 1970, they were much bigger than what the machines could do. When the promises failed, the money stopped.
But the promises weren’t all wrong. Some were only too early.
Today is different. AI already does many things people once only dreamed about. It talks, writes, translates, and finds things in pictures. Millions of people use it every day. Many big promises today start from things AI can already do.
That doesn’t mean every promise will come true. When you hear one, ask: What can AI already do? Who checked it?




1.4.2 - Rules Can Win at Games
A game is a small world. It has clear rules. Every move is on the board. Rules can work well in a small world.

In May 1997, IBM’s computer Deep Blue played the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov. Deep Blue won, \(3\frac{1}{2}\) to \(2\frac{1}{2}\).



Half of Deep Blue: one of its two cabinets, now in a museum. Each cabinet is about as tall as a person. (Photo: James the photographer, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons)



People wrote Deep Blue’s rules for judging a chess position.
Then it checked about 200 million positions every second.
Deep Blue didn’t learn like the drawing AI in Lesson 1.1. It used rules and speed.



Deep Blue could beat the best chess player in the world. But its rules couldn’t tell a cat from a dog. Rules that work in a small world don’t work in the big, messy real world.

No. With all 8 rules, the bot never loses. The best you can do is a tie.
Some rules matter more than others. Turn off Block and the bot doesn’t stop you from winning. Turn off Side and nothing changes.


No one knows. People tried for years and couldn’t write them. A cat can be any color, any size, in any position, in any light. There are too many cases.
That’s why AI changed. In the next lesson, you’ll see what happened when scientists stopped writing rules and started collecting examples.

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
🔥 Warm Up
How did you learn what a dog is? Nobody gave you a rule. You saw many dogs: big dogs, small dogs, dogs in pictures, dogs on the street.
In 2006, a young scientist named Fei-Fei Li had an idea. Maybe computers need the same thing: not rules, but millions of examples.
Today, you do the job that thousands of people did for her project: you label pictures. And you find out that people don’t always agree.
Think about something you learned to recognize as a child: a dog, a car, your mother’s voice, the letter A.
Tell a partner.

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
Did someone give you a rule? Or did you see many examples?
About how many examples do you think you saw?



A lot! Fei-Fei Li says: think of a child’s eyes as a camera that takes about 5 pictures every second. By age 3, the child has seen hundreds of millions of pictures. Children learn from examples, not rules.
Fei-Fei Li thought: computers have rules, but they don’t have enough examples.

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.5.1 - ImageNet
In 2006, Fei-Fei Li, a scientist at Princeton University, started a project called ImageNet. She wanted a giant dataset: pictures of everything in the world, each with a label.





The pictures came from the internet. But the internet doesn’t say what is in each picture. People had to look and decide. Each person saw a word, like chair, and a group of pictures. They clicked every picture that showed a chair.
ImageNet was shared with the world in 2009. It was the biggest set of labeled pictures anyone had made.



1.5.2 - The Big Win in 2012
Every year, scientists entered a contest. Their programs looked at ImageNet pictures and named what was in them.





In 2012, a team from Toronto used a neural network. (You’ll learn how neural networks work in Unit 2.) Their mistakes dropped from about 26% to 15%. Nobody had seen a jump that big.
They trained their network on two GPUs, chips made for video games. A GPU can do thousands of small math problems at the same time.


Lots of data (like ImageNet)
Neural networks that learn from the data
Fast chips (GPUs) to do the math

AI didn’t get better because people wrote better rules. It got better because of examples.


Go is a board game from China. It’s much harder for computers than chess. In 2016, a neural network called AlphaGo played Lee Sedol, one of the best Go players in the world. AlphaGo won, 4 games to 1.
Deep Blue used rules that people wrote (Lesson 1.4). AlphaGo learned from examples. First it learned from games that people played. Then it played millions of games against itself.

🛠️ Try It

There’s no right answer! People decide. And different people decide differently.
ImageNet had this problem too. So the workers got instructions, and several people labeled each picture. If most people agreed, the label stayed.


If the labelers said a hot dog is a sandwich, the AI will say it too. The AI doesn’t know what a sandwich really is. It only knows what people labeled.
What if all the labelers came from one country? The AI would learn their idea of a sandwich. In Unit 4, you’ll see more ways that AI learns unfair patterns.


Have you ever clicked every picture with a traffic light, to prove you aren’t a robot? That test is a CAPTCHA.
Google’s reCAPTCHA uses those clicks to label data for AI. Look at what it asked for, and you can see what AI was learning:

2007: blurry words from old books and newspapers. Computers were learning to read.
From 2012: house numbers, street signs, traffic lights, crosswalks, and buses, from photos of streets. Computers were learning to see a street.

Every time you solved one, you were a labeler too. Nobody paid you.

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
🔥 Warm Up
On November 30, 2022, a company called OpenAI shared a chatbot named ChatGPT. In about two months, around 100 million people used it. At that time, no app had ever grown that fast.
ChatGPT came from an idea that Google scientists shared in 2017. The idea is called attention. You use it every time you read.
Today, you see how attention works. Then you build a sentence the way a chatbot does: one word at a time.
Read these two sentences. What does “it” mean in each one? Write your answers on your sheet.

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.
The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too wide.



In sentence 1, “it” means the animal. Animals get tired. Streets don’t.
In sentence 2, “it” means the street. Streets can be wide. Animals aren’t “too wide” to cross.
Only one word changed. To decide, you looked back at other words in the sentence. You paid attention to the right words.

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.6.1 - Attention (2017)
For a long time, AI read one word at a time. It had trouble remembering the start of a long sentence. In 2017, scientists at Google shared a new kind of neural network. They called it the transformer.
A transformer looks at every word at the same time. For each word, it decides which other words matter most. This is called attention. The scientists’ paper had a famous title: Attention Is All You Need.








1.6.2 - GPT and ChatGPT





A GPT is a large language model. It learned by playing one game, billions of times: predict the next word (like a phone keyboard, when it suggests your next word). When it answers you, it predicts one word, then the next, then the next.

There are many chatbots built this way: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Llama, and more. Most AI tools made for schools are built on top of models like these.

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
🛠️ Try It

1.6.3 - Be the Chatbot: Next Word, by Vote

Everyone writes one next word on a small paper. Don’t talk!
Your teacher counts the votes. The word with the most votes is added to the sentence. Everyone writes it on the sheet.
Do it again for the next word. Keep going until the sentence ends (about 8 words).
Now give the same start to your class AI tool: “Finish this sentence: After school, my friends and I”. Compare its sentence with the class sentence.



Usually it is ordinary. The most common word wins every time, so the sentence uses common words.
Chatbots have the same problem. So they don’t always pick the top word. Sometimes they pick the second or third word, on purpose, to make the writing more interesting.

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Unit 2: Brains and Neural Networks
A real look at how brain cells work, and how computer scientists copied the idea to build AI.
We’ll act out a neural network as a class, watch one learn on screen, and train our own. Then we’ll see how the same idea works inside AI that sees pictures and AI that writes.
By the end of this unit, you’ll be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Explain how a brain cell (neuron) sends a signal
Explain how practice changes the brain
Explain how an artificial neuron copies that idea
Train a neural network and watch it learn
Explain how AI sees pictures and how a chatbot picks its next word

title: Introduction
text:
Topics in This Unit
Simple Rules, Complex Behavior
Watch a wave nobody leads. Make a few rows of Rule 30, explore the other rules, and watch the Game of Life.
Your Brain Is Made of Cells
Catch a falling ruler, pass a squeeze around the room, and learn how a neuron sends a signal.
How Brains Learn
Write with your other hand, meet Pavlov’s dogs, and graph your own learning with mirror drawing.
The Artificial Neuron
Multiply, add, compare. The class fixes a neuron’s weights by hand until it tells Fighters from Wizards.
Train a Human Neural Network
The class becomes a network with a hidden layer. It starts with bad weights and learns by fixing its own mistakes.
Build a Real AI
Six steps to build an AI. Train a real neural network on 300 creatures, and watch its weights change.
Train Your Own AI
Teach Teachable Machine your own hand signs. Then try to fool it.
How AI Sees
A picture is a grid of numbers. A filter is a neuron that finds edges, and each layer finds something more complicated: edges, corners, then whole things.
How Chatbots Work
Build a tiny chatbot that counts which word comes next. Roll dice to make it write, then see how a real chatbot does the same job with a network.

title: 2.1 - Simple Rules, Complex Behavior
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In Unit 1, rules failed. Nobody could write rules for “cat.”
But rules have a surprise. A very simple rule can make something very complicated. Nobody plans it. It just happens.
Your brain works a little like this. Each brain cell follows simple rules. About 86 billion of them together make you. Today, you follow simple rules, then test hundreds of them.
Watch a crowd make a wave. Every person follows one rule:
If there’s time, try it yourselves. Sit in a row and follow the same rule. Even 4 people can pass a small wave.

title: 2.1 - Simple Rules, Complex Behavior
text:
When the person on your left raises their hands, raise your hands. Put them down quickly.



  
    ▶ Start the wave
    Speed

Nobody! Each person only watched one neighbor. The person you watched only went up and down. The wave moved across the row, but no person did.
When many simple parts make something bigger that nobody planned, we call it emergence.

title: 2.1 - Simple Rules, Complex Behavior
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.1.1 - One Row, One Rule
Stephen Wolfram started Wolfram Research, the company that makes the math program Mathematica. He spent years on one question: how can very simple rules make very complicated things? He studied rows of squares like this one.
Picture a row of squares. Each square is black or white. Every square looks at itself and its two neighbors. Then the rule card says what color it will be in the next row.





There are only 8 possible patterns of 3 squares. So a rule card has 8 answers. This card is called Rule 90. A world like this is called a cellular automaton.

On your sheet, start with one black square in the middle of the top row. Make the next 4 rows with the Rule 90 card. Look at each square and its two neighbors in the row above. (Outside the grid, everything is white.) What shape is starting to appear?




2.1.2 - One Small Change: Rule 30
Now change just 2 of the 8 answers on the card. The new card is Rule 30:





Wolfram studied Rule 30 in 1983. Here it’s after 80 rows, starting from one black square:





The rule is tiny. But the middle of the picture looks random. Even Wolfram can’t say what row 1,000 will look like. The only way to know is to make all 999 rows before it.
Nature makes patterns like this. A sea snail’s shell grows at its edge, one thin row at a time. Each cell on the edge makes color or doesn’t, depending on its neighbors. That’s a row of cells following a rule! Look at the shell of this cone snail:



A textile cone snail (Conus textile) on the Great Barrier Reef. Look at the triangles on its shell. Do they look like Rule 30? (Photo: Richard Ling, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons)



Simple rules can make behavior that is just as complicated as anything else. Wolfram calls this the Principle of Computational Equivalence. He thinks a row of cells, the weather, and a brain can all be equally complicated. Not every scientist agrees.
This matters for AI. A neural network is made of tiny parts that follow simple rules. So is your brain.

text:
🛠️ Try It

2.1.3 - Explore the Rules
There are 256 different rule cards. Most of them were never studied by anyone before computers. Use the tool in 2.1.2 with a partner.


Try 110, 4, 150, and 30. For each rule, circle what it looks like on your sheet: never changes, a pattern that repeats, chaos, or complex.
Make your own rule. Click the bottom squares on the rule card to change them. What’s your rule’s number? What kind is it?
Traffic! Choose 184 and Start: random, then press Draw it. Each black square is a car. A car moves one square to the right if the square in front of it is empty. Each row is the same road, one moment later. Find a traffic jam: a thick dark stripe. As you go down the picture, which way does the jam move?



Backward! No car ever moves backward. But a jam does. Cars at the front of the jam drive away, and new cars join at the back. Real traffic jams on highways do the same thing. Nobody planned it. It emerges from one simple rule.
You can’t tell what a rule will do by reading its card. Rule 110 is the strangest: it makes shapes that move and crash into each other. Scientists proved that Rule 110 can do any calculation a computer can do, if the row is long enough. You have to run a rule and look.



2.1.4 - Simple Rules Everywhere
Your teacher shows these on the screen.
A flock of birds. Thousands of birds can turn together like one animal. There is no leader. Each bird follows 3 simple rules about the birds near it:

The Game of Life. This is a grid, not a row. Each square follows simple rules about its 8 neighbors. Your teacher adds a glider and presses Run. Watch the glider. Look closely at one square. Does it move?

Your brain has about 86 billion cells called neurons. A neuron is a cell that sends signals.

2.2.2 - How a Signal Moves

Signals come in through the dendrites.
The cell body adds them up. If the total is big enough, the neuron fires. If not, nothing happens. There’s no “half fire.”
When it fires, an electric signal runs down the axon.
At the synapse, the neuron lets out tiny chemicals. They carry the signal across the gap to the next neuron.

title: 2.3 - How Brains Learn
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Think of something that was very hard the first time: riding a bike, writing in a new alphabet, a move in a sport. Now it’s easy. You don’t even think about it.
What changed? Not your hands. Your brain changed. Practice made some connections between your neurons stronger.
Today, you watch your own brain learn something new, and you measure it.
Write your full name with your other hand (the one you don’t usually write with). Your partner times you.

title: 2.3 - How Brains Learn
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.3.1 - Practice Makes Connections Stronger
Did you get faster with your other hand? Your hand didn’t change in 3 tries. Your brain did.
When you do something new, a group of neurons fires together. When you do it again and again, the synapses between those neurons get stronger. The signal passes more easily. The skill gets faster and smoother.
Scientists say it with a short rhyme:

Neurons that fire together, wire together.

When you stop practicing, unused connections can get weaker. That’s why you forget things you never use.

Ivan Pavlov was a scientist in Russia. He studied dogs.



A drawing of a Pavlov experiment. A tube carries saliva from the dog’s cheek to a scale on the wall, so the scientists can measure how much the dog drools. The person sits behind a wall, so the dog can’t see him. (Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0)



Dogs drool (make saliva in their mouths) when they see food. Nobody teaches them this.
Pavlov’s team played a sound, a clicking metronome, right before they gave the dogs food. They did this many times.
Soon, the dogs drooled when they heard the clicking, with no food at all.

The dogs’ brains connected the sound with food. This kind of learning is called conditioning.


In a brain, learning means changing how strong the connections are between neurons.
AI copies this idea. In a neural network, the strength of each connection is a number called a weight. Learning means changing the weights. You’ll see this in the next lesson.

title: 2.4 - The Artificial Neuron
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A real neuron takes in signals, adds them up, and fires if the total is big enough.
In 1943, two scientists, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, wrote this idea as math. In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt built a machine from it. It was called the perceptron. (The 1958 newspaper story in Lesson 1.4 was about this machine.)
That simple idea is the building block of every neural network today. Today, you’ll build one by hand.
These cards are for made-up creatures. Each card shows two numbers, as stars: Strength (how hard it hits) and Magic.
One is a Fighter. One is a Wizard. Which is which? Tell a partner why.

text:
👥 Learn Together

2.4.1 - Multiply, Add, Compare
An artificial neuron does three things:






Multiply each input by its weight.
Add them up.
Compare the total with the threshold. If the total is more than the threshold, the neuron fires: Fighter. If not: Wizard.

\[\text{total} = (\text{Strength} \times \text{Strength weight}) + (\text{Magic} \times \text{Magic weight})\]
A weight can be negative. Here the Magic weight is \(-1\). It says: more Magic makes me LESS likely to say Fighter.







Real neuron

An artificial neuron is only multiply, add, compare. That’s all. A neural network is many of these, connected together.



2.4.2 - From One Neuron to a Network
One neuron makes one small decision. A neural network connects many neurons. They’re arranged in rows called layers.






The input layer holds the numbers that go in. Here, they’re the two numbers from a card.
Every neuron in the hidden layer gets every input. Each one multiplies, adds, and compares, like the neuron above. Each one has its own weights. Its answer isn’t “Fighter” or “Wizard”. Its answer goes to the next layer as an input.
The output layer gives the answer. There’s one neuron for each possible answer. The one with the biggest total wins.

Every line is a weight. Count them: \(2 \times 3 + 3 \times 2 = 12\) weights. The chatbots you use have billions of weights and many hidden layers.

You see the numbers that go in and the answer that comes out. You don’t see what the middle neurons decide. Nobody tells them what to look for, either. They find it while the network learns. In Lesson 2.5, the class becomes a network and watches this happen.

One neuron can’t learn this rule. Today, the class becomes a real network, with a hidden layer. It starts with bad weights, and it learns by fixing its own mistakes.

title: 2.5 - Train a Human Neural Network
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.5.1 - The Class Network





Each neuron is a team of students. Each team writes its numbers on the sheet. The tool in 2.5.3 shows every number on the screen. The starting numbers are wrong on purpose.
To run one card:

Read the card. Strong Strength? Strong Magic? Each answer is 1 (yes) or 0 (no).
Hidden teams: add the weights of the inputs that are 1. (An input that’s 0 adds nothing.) If your total is more than your threshold, stand up. You fired!
Output team: add the weights of the hidden teams that are standing. More than your threshold? Say “Can join!” If not, say “Can’t join.”
Check: unfold the card. Was the network right?




2.5.2 - The Fix Rule, and Who’s to Blame
When the network is wrong, one neuron changes. Every neuron uses the same fix rule:







What happened
What that neuron does




It should have fired, but it didn’t
ADD: +1 to the weight of each input that was 1. Threshold −1.


It fired, but it shouldn’t have
SUBTRACT: −1 from the weight of each input that was 1. Threshold +1.



An input that was 0 didn’t cause the mistake, so its weight stays the same.
But which neuron should change? Play Who’s to Blame?


Look at the two hidden neurons. Which one was least sure? That’s the one whose total was closest to its threshold.
Imagine that neuron changed its answer. Would the network be right now?
Yes: that hidden neuron uses the fix rule. No: the output neuron uses the fix rule.



Konik has Strength 4 stars and Magic 2 stars. Strong Strength = 1. Strong Magic = 0.

Hidden 1: total \(= -1\). More than 1? No. It stays seated (0).
Hidden 2: total \(= 0\). More than 1? No. It stays seated (0).
Output: nobody is standing, so its total \(= 0\). More than 1? No: “Can’t join.”
Check: Konik is a Fighter. It can join. Wrong!
Who’s to blame? Hidden 1 is 2 away from its threshold (\(-1\) to \(1\)). Hidden 2 is 1 away (\(0\) to \(1\)). Hidden 2 is least sure.
If Hidden 2 stood up, the output total would be 1. More than 1? No. Still wrong. So the output neuron fixes itself.
It should have fired: ADD. Both of its inputs were 0, so its weights stay the same. Its threshold goes from 1 to 0.


This is a simple version of a real method from 1988, called MADALINE Rule II. Bernard Widrow and Rodney Winter made it.

Real networks share the blame with backpropagation. After a mistake, the computer works out how much each weight caused it, from the last layer back to the first. Then it changes every weight a little. It does this billions of times.


The hidden neurons learned to …

title: 2.6 - Build a Real AI
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In Lesson 2.5, the class trained a network of 3 neurons on 8 cards. It took about 20 minutes, and every step was done by hand.
A computer can do the same work on 300 creatures, with many neurons, in a few seconds. Today, you build it yourself. You’ll watch its weights change while it learns.
Your job is to predict what will happen, then train the network, and then test it.
The class network needed 2 passes through 8 cards. Each card took about 1 minute.
The computer trains on 240 creatures, and does 300 passes. How long would that take by hand? Work it out with a partner.

title: 2.6 - Build a Real AI
text:
\(240 \times 300 = 72{,}000\) cards. At 1 minute each, that’s \(72{,}000\) minutes: about 1,200 hours, or 50 days without sleeping!
A computer does it in a few seconds.

title: 2.6 - Build a Real AI
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.6.1 - Six Steps to Build an AI






Get data. The dataset has 300 creatures, the same made-up creatures from the cards. Each one has 6 numbers: Strength, Magic, Speed, Toughness, Height, and Weight. Each one also has a type and a home.
Ask a question. For example: Is it a Fighter or a Wizard?
Split the data. Most creatures go into the training data. The rest go into the test data. The network never trains on the test data.
Build the network. Choose how many neurons go in its hidden layer.
Train. Each pass, the network looks at every training creature. Then it changes every weight a little, to make fewer mistakes. This is backpropagation, the computer’s way to play Who’s to Blame (Lesson 2.5).
Test, then use it. Check it on the test creatures. Then ask it about any creature.


Imagine you get the answers to a test the day before. You get 100%. Did you learn the math? Maybe not! You might have just memorized the answers.
An AI can do the same thing. The only fair check is data it has never seen.



2.6.2 - How to Read the Network
The tool draws the network while it trains.

Left: the inputs, the numbers that go in. Middle: the hidden neurons. Right: the answers.

On a 2-number question, each hidden neuron is a small square. It’s a tiny map: Strength goes right, Magic goes up. It’s blue where that neuron fires, and orange where it doesn’t. Each one draws one line, like the neuron in Lesson 2.4.

The class neuron from Lesson 2.4 got about 91% of all 140 Fighters and Wizards right. This network gets about the same on the test creatures. Look at the big map: the border is almost a straight line. Fighter or Wizard really is a one-line question, so more neurons don’t help much.

title: 2.8 - How AI Sees
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In Lesson 2.7, your AI told Rock from Paper from Scissors. But to a computer, a photo is a grid of numbers. Nothing else.
So how does a network find a hand in a grid of numbers? It uses neurons, like the ones you built. And it uses layers: each layer finds something a little more complicated than the layer before.
Your sheet has a grid of numbers. Color every square with a 1. Leave every 0 white. What is the picture?

title: 2.8 - How AI Sees
text:
You turned numbers into a picture. A computer screen does the same thing millions of times a second.
A camera does the opposite. It turns a picture into numbers.

title: 2.8 - How AI Sees
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.8.1 - Pixels Are Numbers
Zoom in on any photo and you see tiny squares. Each square is a pixel.

In a black-and-white picture, each pixel is one number: 0 is black, 255 is white, and the numbers between are grays.
In a color picture, each pixel is three numbers: how much red, green, and blue.
A phone photo can have about 12 million pixels. That’s about 36 million numbers!




2.8.2 - A Filter Is a Neuron
Where does a picture change fast from dark to light? That’s an edge. Edges show where things begin and end.
To find edges, a vision network uses a filter. A filter is a neuron with 9 inputs: a 3 by 3 patch of the picture. Its 9 weights are the filter’s numbers.






Multiply the 9 picture numbers by the 9 weights, and add. That’s the same multiply, add, compare as the neuron in Lesson 2.4.
If the total is far from 0, the neuron fires: there’s an edge here. (A big minus number is an edge too, going the other way: light to dark.) Where the picture is the same on both sides, the \(-1\)s and \(+1\)s cancel. The total is 0: no edge.
Then the same neuron moves one square over and looks again. It does this at every spot. Its answers make a new picture: a map of the edges.




2.8.3 - Layers: Edges, Then Shapes, Then Things
Layer 1 finds edges. Layer 2 doesn’t look at the picture. It looks at layer 1’s maps. Where an up-and-down edge meets a side-to-side edge, a layer 2 neuron finds a corner.
Every layer builds on the one before: edges, then corners and curves, then patterns, then parts, then whole things. Here’s what real neurons look for, layer by layer:



What neurons look for, from early layers to later ones, in a real network called GoogLeNet. It learned from millions of ImageNet pictures (Lesson 1.5). Scientists asked each neuron: what picture makes you fire the most? Then the computer drew it. (From “Feature Visualization” by Chris Olah, Alexander Mordvintsev, and Ludwig Schubert, Distill, 2017, CC BY 4.0. Cropped and labeled.)



Nobody. Nobody told this network to look for stripes, flowers, or dog noses. Training found every one of its filters, the same way the network in Lesson 2.6 found its weights.
The first layer of almost every vision network ends up finding edges, like the filters you’ll try today.



Self-driving cars find lanes, signs, other cars, and people.
Phones find your face to unlock.
Doctors use it to look for problems in X-rays.
Farms use it to find sick plants.

title: 2.9 - How Chatbots Work
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In Lesson 1.6, you learned that a chatbot writes one word at a time. It predicts the next word, again and again.
But how does it choose the next word? Today, you build the simplest chatbot possible. It does only one thing: it counts which word comes next. Then it writes. You’ll be surprised what counting can do, and what it can’t.

2.9.1 - Count What Comes Next

The chatbot turns counts into chances. After “like”, the next word was “rice” 2 times out of 3: that’s 67%. This list of chances is the chatbot’s answer, like the answers of the network in Lesson 2.6.
To write, it starts with a word and looks it up. It picks a next word, using the chances. Then it looks that word up, and so on.

Start with My: My → friend → likes → rice → and → beans → end.
“My friend likes rice and beans.” That sentence is not in the training text! The chatbot made something new by mixing pieces it had seen.




2.9.2 - From Counting to ChatGPT
A real chatbot is a large language model (Lesson 1.6). It has the same goal: predict the next word. But it doesn’t keep a table. It’s a neural network.



This shows the idea. The percentages are made up.



The words so far go in.
They pass through many layers. Attention (Lesson 1.6) lets each word look back at the other words.
The output layer has one neuron for every word it knows, about 100,000. Each one says how likely its word is to come next.
The chatbot picks a word, adds it, and runs the whole network again for the next word.

The answers look like your table’s chances. But a real chatbot looks back at thousands of words, not just one.

text:

Maria types: “Tell me about dogs.” She gets a long page about the history of dogs, dog breeds, and dog food. She can’t use most of it.
Kofi types: “I am in 10th grade. I am writing a 1-minute speech about why dogs make good pets. Give me 3 reasons, with one short example each. Use simple words.” He gets exactly what he needs. Same chatbot. Different question.

text:
“Help with my essay.” (Tomás has an essay about his home country due tomorrow. He needs a good first sentence.)
“Explain volcanoes.” (Amina is in 6th grade. She has a test on Friday. She reads English slowly.)

You know Tomás, Amina, and Lin. The chatbot doesn’t. It only has the words they typed. Everything else, it has to guess.

title: 3.1 - Asking Good Questions
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.1.1 - What Is a Prompt?
A prompt is what you type to tell an AI what you want. It can be a question, a job, or both.
Remember Lesson 1.6: a chatbot predicts the next word, again and again. It uses every word you typed to make its prediction. Short prompt: it predicts an answer for an average person. Clear prompt: it predicts an answer for you.



3.1.2 - The Three Parts of a Good Prompt
Here is Kofi’s prompt again, in color:

I am in 10th grade. Give me 3 reasons why dogs make good pets, with one short example each. This is for a 1-minute speech. Use simple words.









Part
The question it answers
Kofi’s prompt

Give 3 reasons dogs make good pets


Context
Who are you? What is it for?
10th grade, a 1-minute speech


Format

3 reasons, one example each, simple words




Task, context, format. You don’t need all three every time. But when an answer isn’t useful, one of them is usually missing.




3.1.3 - Keep Your Private Information Private

An AI tool may save what you type. A person at the company may read it. So never type:

your name, or anyone else’s name
pictures of yourself or other people
your address, phone number, birthday, or student number
passwords
private facts about another person

For context, “I am in high school” is enough. The AI doesn’t need to know which high school.


Your class AI tool is Raina, in MagicSchool. Your teacher will show you how to open it. In this book, it’s called your class AI tool.
Many popular chatbots have age rules. ChatGPT says users must be at least 13, and users under 18 need a parent’s permission. Claude.ai says users must be 18. Use the tool your school gives you.

🔭 Explore More: prompts in your language, and a fourth trick. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more.

title: 3.2 - Keep Talking
text:
🔥 Warm Up
When you ask a teacher a question and you don’t understand the answer, you don’t walk away. You say, “Can you say that another way?” or “Can you show me an example?”
You can do the same with a chatbot. The first answer is only a first try. The second and third answers are often much better.
Today you learn the follow-up questions that turn a bad answer into a useful one.
A student asked a chatbot, “What is photosynthesis?” Here is an answer like the one they got:
On your sheet, circle 3 hard words. What would you say to the chatbot next?

title: 3.2 - Keep Talking
text:
Photosynthesis is the biochemical process by which photoautotrophic organisms convert electromagnetic radiation into chemical energy, synthesizing glucose from carbon dioxide and water while releasing molecular oxygen as a byproduct.



The student typed: “Explain it in simple words. I am in high school and I am learning English. Use 3 short sentences.”
The new answer: Plants make their own food. They use sunlight, water, and air. They give off oxygen, the gas we breathe.
Same facts. Now the student can use them.

title: 3.2 - Keep Talking
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.2.1 - The Chat Is the Prompt
When you send a new message, the chatbot doesn’t read only your new message. It reads the whole chat again, from the top. Then it predicts its answer.





So your follow-up question works because the old messages are still part of the prompt. The words a chatbot can read at one time are called its context window.

A new chat starts over. The chatbot can’t see your old chat. If you need the context, type it again.




3.2.2 - Follow-Up Moves








Move
Say this
Use it when the answer is …




Simpler
“Explain it in simple words.”
too hard to read


Shorter
“Say it in 3 sentences.”
too long


Example
“Give me an example.”
too general


Why?
“Why? Show me the steps.”
hard to believe


Fix it
“That is not what I meant. I meant …”
about the wrong thing


New shape
“Make it a table.” or “Make it a list.”
hard to use


Language
“Say it in English and in Arabic.”
hard to understand in English

title: 3.2 - Keep Talking
text:
🛠️ Try It

3.2.3 - The Follow-Up Challenge
Work with a partner, or in a group of 3.


Choose a hard topic from another class: photosynthesis, the water cycle, slope, the U.S. Constitution, or your own idea.
Ask your class AI tool: “What is …?” Read the answer.
On your sheet, give the answer a score from 1 to 5. (1 = I can’t use this. 5 = I can use this today.)
Use one follow-up move. Score the new answer.
Do it 2 more times, with different moves. Which move helped the most?

title: 3.2 - Keep Talking
text:
💬 Talk About It
You kept asking until the answer was useful. When is it better to keep talking, and when is it better to start a new chat? Should it be your job to keep asking, or should the AI get it right the first time?


The follow-up move that helped me most was … , because …
A chatbot remembers the chat because …
I would start a new chat when …
It (is / isn’t) fair that I have to keep asking, because …

title: 3.2 - Keep Talking
text:
🚀 Go Further

Test the picture in 3.2.1 for yourself.

In the same chat as your follow-up challenge, ask: “What topic did I ask about?” What does it say?
Open a new chat. Ask the same question. What does it say now?
Write what happened on your sheet. Use the picture in 3.2.1 to explain why.



Type: “You are a job interviewer at a grocery store. Ask me one question at a time. Wait for my answer. After each answer, give me one tip.” Keep talking for 5 questions. What was the best tip? (Don’t type your name or anything else about who you are.)


Type: “Quiz me on the water cycle. Ask one question at a time. Tell me if I am right before the next question.” How is this different from just reading the answer?


🔭 Explore More: why “Are you sure?” can change a right answer, and chatbot memory. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more.

title: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Two students get the same job: write a paragraph about a place that matters to them.
Ahmed types, “Write a paragraph about a place that matters to me.” In 5 seconds, he has a nice paragraph about a quiet park where he likes to think. He has never been to that park.
Sara writes about her grandmother’s kitchen: the smell of bread, the radio, the blue door. Then she asks the AI, “What is one thing I could make clearer?” She fixes two sentences. Who wrote something true? Who got better at writing?
Read the story at the top again. Answer on your sheet:
crumbs: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI

title: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI
text:
Whose paragraph is true?
Who practiced writing?
Did both of them use AI?


When you write, you decide what you mean. You choose the words. You put ideas in order. That’s how you get better at thinking.
If the AI writes it, the AI got the practice. You didn’t.
crumbs: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI

title: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.3.1 - The AI Use Ladder
There are many ways to use AI for writing. Each step up the ladder, the AI does more of the work.





Each assignment should say which step is OK. If it does not say, ask your teacher before you use AI.

Using AI on a step that isn’t allowed, and turning the work in as your own, is plagiarism. It’s the same as copying from a friend.




3.3.2 - Ask for Feedback, Then Decide
If you ask, “Make my paragraph better,” the AI will often write a new paragraph. Then it isn’t yours anymore. Ask for feedback instead:

Don’t rewrite my paragraph. I am in high school and I am learning English. Tell me 2 things that are good and 2 things I could make better. Use simple words. Here is my paragraph: …

AI advice isn’t always right. You’re the boss of your writing. For each piece of advice, you decide:







Decision
When




✅ Keep it
It makes your meaning clearer.


✏️ Change it
The idea is good, but you want to say it your way.


❌ Skip it
It’s wrong, or it changes what you meant.
crumbs: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI

title: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI
text:
🛠️ Try It

3.3.3 - Write, Ask, Decide
Work with a partner. (If there’s an odd number, make one group of 3.)


Write a draft: 5 sentences about a place that matters to you. You can plan in your home language first.
Read your paragraph to your partner. Your partner says one thing they liked.
Copy the feedback prompt from 3.3.2 into your class AI tool. Add your paragraph at the end.
On your sheet, write each piece of advice. Mark it Keep, Change, or Skip. Write why.



Write about a place, not an address. Don’t use any names: write “my grandmother” or “my friend” instead.
crumbs: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI

title: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI
text:
💬 Talk About It
When is using AI for writing OK, and when is it cheating? If AI can write well, why should people still learn to write?


Using AI is OK when … , and it’s cheating when …
I kept the advice to … because …
I skipped the advice to … because …
People should still learn to write because …
crumbs: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI

title: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI
text:
🚀 Go Further


Use your Keep and Change decisions. Write your new paragraph on your sheet.
At the end, write an AI note. It’s short and honest. It says what you did and what the AI did. For example:


AI note: I wrote this paragraph myself. I used my class AI tool for feedback. I kept 1 idea: I added the smell of the bread. I skipped 1 idea, because it changed what I meant.


Read your new paragraph to your partner. What changed?



As a class, decide which step of the ladder is OK for different jobs: a journal, a science report, a job application, a text to a friend. Make a poster.


Ask the AI to write 5 sentences about a place that matters to it. Give your paragraph and the AI’s paragraph to a partner, with no names. Can they tell which is which? How?


🔭 Explore More: your writing voice, and feedback in your language. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more.
crumbs: 3.3 - Writing with AI, Not by AI

title: 3.4 - Research and Checking
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In 2023, two lawyers in New York had to write a report for a court. One of them asked ChatGPT to find old court cases that agreed with them.
ChatGPT gave him six cases. Each one had a name, a date, and quotes. None of the six cases were real. The judge fined the lawyers and their law firm $5,000.
The lawyer said he didn’t know a chatbot could make things up. Today you learn to check, so this never happens to you.
Two of these court cases are real. One was made up by ChatGPT for the lawyers in 2023. Which one is made up? How could you find out?

title: 3.4 - Research and Checking
text:
Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
Varghese v. China Southern Airlines (2019)
Miranda v. Arizona (1966)


Number 2 is made up. It was one of the six fake cases. It looks just like a real case name: two names, “v.”, and a year. That’s why it fooled the lawyer.
To find out, you could search for it. The real cases are on many trusted websites. The fake one shows up only in news stories about the fake cases.

title: 3.4 - Research and Checking
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.4.1 - Why a Chatbot Makes Things Up
A chatbot predicts likely words. It doesn’t look up each fact in a book. A fake court case has the same shape as a real one, so the fake words look very likely.
When AI writes something false as if it were true, it’s called a hallucination. The chatbot doesn’t know it’s wrong. It sounds just as sure as when it’s right. (You’ll study this more in Lesson 4.1.)



3.4.2 - Lateral Reading
Professional fact-checkers don’t read one page carefully from top to bottom. They open new tabs and see what other sources say. This is called lateral reading. (“Lateral” means “to the side.”)


Choose one fact.
Open a new tab. Search for the fact.
Find it in 2 trusted sources that agree.
Mark it: ✅ found in 2 sources, ❌ wrong, or ❓ can’t find.










Usually trusted
Use with care
Be careful




government websites (.gov)
Wikipedia: a good start, then check the links at the bottom
social media posts


encyclopedias, like Britannica
a blog by one person
a website that sells something


big news organizations
a video on YouTube or TikTok
a chatbot answer with no source


museums and universities (.edu)

title: 3.4 - Research and Checking
text:
🛠️ Try It

3.4.3 - Check the Chatbot
Our school is named after Frederick Douglass. Let’s check what a chatbot says about him. Work with a partner, or in a group of 3.


Ask your class AI tool: “Tell me 5 facts about Frederick Douglass.”
Write the 5 facts on your sheet.
Choose 3 facts. Check each one with lateral reading. Use the “Usually trusted” sources. Mark ✅, ❌, or ❓.

title: 3.4 - Research and Checking
text:
💬 Talk About It
AI can make things up, and it sounds sure when it does. Should students use AI for research at all? If yes, how?


The chatbot got … right, and it got … wrong.
A source I trust is … because …
Students (should / shouldn’t) use AI for research, because …
Before I use a fact from AI, I will …

title: 3.4 - Research and Checking
text:
📺 Watch

🏫 At school: watch this video on yout-ube.com
While you watch: What do fact-checkers do that most people don’t?
Captions in your language: Press CC, then ⚙️ Settings, then Subtitles/CC, then Auto-translate.

title: 3.4 - Research and Checking
text:
🚀 Go Further


Ask your class AI tool: “Give me 3 sources about Frederick Douglass.” (If it won’t give links, ask for book titles and authors.)
Check each one. Is it real? Search for it, or look in the school library catalog.
Does the source really say what the AI said?
Sort the sources on your sheet: usually trusted, use with care, or be careful.



Find a surprising claim that many people are sharing online. Use lateral reading to check it. Is it true, false, or missing important facts? Present what you found in 1 minute.


🔭 Explore More: chatbots that search the web, and harder topics to check. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more.

title: 3.5 - AI and Your Language
text:
🔥 Warm Up
About 14 languages are spoken at our school. AI can translate many of them. It’s very good at some languages and weak at others.
How good is it at your language? The people who made the AI can’t tell you. They don’t speak it. You do.
Today, you’re the expert. You grade the AI.
On your sheet, write “Good morning! How are you?” in every language you know.
Then share. Your teacher makes a list on the board of every language in the room. How many are there?

title: 3.5 - AI and Your Language
text: If you speak only English, you’re still the expert on English. Today, pair up with someone who speaks another language. You’ll learn some of it.

title: 3.5 - AI and Your Language
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.5.1 - How AI Learned to Translate
People didn’t write rules for every language. The AI learned from examples: millions of texts that exist in two languages. A website in English and Spanish. A report from the United Nations in six languages. A book and its translation.
An AI is only as good as its training examples. Some languages have a lot of writing online. Some have very little. A language with little writing for AI to learn from is called a low-resource language. AI makes more mistakes in these languages.

About half of all websites are in English. Spanish, German, Japanese, and French are next, with about 5% each. Many languages are on less than 1 in 1,000 websites. (Source: W3Techs, October 2026.)
Google Translate works with almost 250 languages. Your class AI tool may work with fewer.




3.5.2 - Hard in Every Language

Idioms: “It’s raining cats and dogs” means it’s raining very hard. A word-by-word translation makes no sense.
Words with two meanings: “a break” can be a rest, or a time when someone is less strict with you.

To check a translation, translate it back: English → your language → English again. If the meaning changed, something went wrong. This is back translation. It’s a good test, but the best test is a person who speaks the language. That’s you.

title: 3.5 - AI and Your Language
text:
🛠️ Try It

3.5.3 - Grade the AI
Work with a partner who speaks the same language, if you can. If you speak only English, work with a partner who speaks another language. You write; they grade.


Translate each sentence below into your language with Google Translate.
Grade each translation: 3 = right and sounds natural, 2 = I understand it, but it sounds strange, 1 = wrong.
Choose one translation. Back-translate it into English. Did the meaning change?
Add your scores to the class chart on the board.


The sentences:
A. The library opens at 8 o’clock. B. Please bring your permission slip by Friday. C. It’s raining cats and dogs. D. My teacher gave me a break. E. A sentence you would really need to say. (At the doctor? At a store?)

Google Translate and your class AI tool send your words to a company’s computers. Don’t type names or private information, like a letter from a doctor or your address.

title: 3.5 - AI and Your Language
text:
💬 Talk About It
Look at the class chart. Which language did AI do best? Worst? Why?
Should a hospital or a court use AI to translate? When do you need a human translator?


AI did best in … , maybe because …
AI made a mistake in my language when …
A hospital (should / shouldn’t) use AI translation, because …
A human translator is needed when …

title: 3.5 - AI and Your Language
text:
🚀 Go Further


Translate the same 5 sentences with your class AI tool.
Grade each one: 3, 2, or 1.
Compare with your Google Translate grades. Which tool is better for your language? Is it better for every sentence?



Collect words and sentences the AI got wrong in each language. Write the wrong translation, the right one, and why the AI made the mistake. Share it with the ELL teachers.


Google Translate can listen and speak. Say a sentence in your language. Does it understand you? Does it understand your partner? Does it work better for some voices?


🔭 Explore More: how translation led to chatbots, and more hard cases. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more.

title: 3.6 - AI and Math
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A calculator from 1975 can do \(3847 \times 29\) and get it right every time. Some of the most powerful AI in the world can solve very hard math contest problems. And yet a chatbot can still get a long multiplication problem wrong, and sound completely sure.
How can that be? Today you find out, and you test it yourself.
A student asked a chatbot to solve \(3x + 5 = 20\). Here are its steps. One step is wrong. Which one?

title: 3.6 - AI and Math
text:
Step
Work




1
\(3x + 5 = 20\)


2
\(3x = 25\)


3
\(x = \dfrac{25}{3}\)




Step 2 is wrong. To undo \(+5\), you subtract 5 from both sides: \(3x = 15\). Then \(x = 5\).
Check by plugging in: \(3(5) + 5 = 15 + 5 = 20\). ✅

title: 3.6 - AI and Math
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.6.1 - Rules and Predictions
Remember Lesson 1.1: some computers follow rules, and some learn from examples.






A calculator follows the rule for multiplying. It does the same steps every time.
A chatbot predicts the answer, one token at a time, like words. On small problems, its guesses are almost always right. On long problems, one bad guess makes the whole answer wrong.

This picture shows the idea. Real chatbots split numbers into pieces in different ways.

In July 2025, AI from Google DeepMind and OpenAI scored at gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad. It’s a contest for the best high school math students in the world.
Many AI tools now use a calculator or computer code behind the scenes for arithmetic. Some don’t. Even the best ones still make mistakes. Always check.




3.6.2 - Three Ways to Check








Way
How
Example: is \(3847 \times 29 = 111563\)?




Estimate
Round, then do it in your head. Is the answer close?
\(4000 \times 30 = 120000\). Close! ✅


Calculator
Do it again with a tool that follows rules.
\(111563\) ✅


Plug it in
Put the answer back in the problem. Does it work?
\(111563 \div 29 = 3847\) ✅

title: 3.6 - AI and Math
text:
🛠️ Try It

3.6.3 - Test the Chatbot
Work with a partner.


Ask your class AI tool each problem below. Ask for only the answer, with no steps.
Check each answer with a calculator.
Mark it ✅ or ❌ on your sheet.
Add your results to the class chart. Which problems did the AI get wrong most often?





Problem
Size




\(23 \times 47\)
small


\(3847 \times 29\)
medium


\(48213 \times 7956\)
big


\(8374615 \times 293847\)
very big




That’s a good result too! Write it down. Your class AI tool may use a calculator behind the scenes. Try asking: “Did you use a calculator for that?” Then check its answer to that question.

title: 3.6 - AI and Math
text:
💬 Talk About It
Should students be allowed to use AI on math homework? When does it help you learn, and when does it stop you from learning?


The AI got the … problem (right / wrong), because …
A calculator is better for arithmetic because …
AI helps me learn math when …
AI stops me from learning when …

title: 3.6 - AI and Math
text:
🚀 Go Further

If AI does your homework, you didn’t learn it. Then the test comes, and the AI isn’t there. So ask for a hint instead:

I am learning to solve equations. Don’t give me the answer. Give me one hint for the first step of \(2x - 7 = 11\). Then wait for me to try.


Use this prompt. Don’t let the AI give you the answer.
Write each hint and each of your steps on your sheet.
Check your answer by plugging it in.

You can also ask AI to check your work: “Here are my steps. Tell me which step is wrong, but do not fix it.”


Ask the very big problem in 3 new chats. Did you get the same answer each time? Why could a chatbot give different answers to the same question? (Hint: Lesson 2.9.)


Ask: “A farmer has 15 cows. All but 8 run away. How many are left?” Is the AI right? (The answer is 8.) Write your own trick word problem and test it.


🔭 Explore More: why numbers are hard for chatbots, and math in your language. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more.

title: 3.7 - Making Pictures with AI
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Type “an orange cat reading a book in a library, watercolor.” Wait a few seconds. A picture appears. Nobody drew it. It didn’t exist before.
How? The AI starts with static, like an old TV with no signal. Then it removes a little static at a time, again and again, until a picture is left.
Look at the first three squares on your sheet. Cover the last one. At which step can you guess the picture? Write your guess.

title: 3.7 - Making Pictures with AI
text:
At step 0, there’s no picture at all. It’s only noise. At step 3, maybe you see a dark shape. At step 6, most people can see it. The details come last.
An image generator works the same way, but it doesn’t know the picture ahead of time. It has to guess it.

title: 3.7 - Making Pictures with AI
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.7.1 - From Noise to Picture





An image generator learns in two parts.
Training. People collect millions of pictures, each with words that describe it. The computer adds noise to each picture, a little at a time, until only noise is left. A neural network practices guessing: which part of this is noise? It practices millions of times.
Making a picture. Now you type words. The AI starts with pure noise. The network guesses which part is noise, and removes a little of it. It does this again and again, often 20 to 50 times. Your words guide every guess. This is called diffusion.

The AI doesn’t copy a picture or glue pieces together. It starts from noise and removes it, step by step, guided by what it learned from millions of pictures.




3.7.2 - Why Every Picture Is Different
Every time you press the button, the AI starts from new random noise. So the same prompt makes a different picture each time. (Like the chatbot that picks by chance, in Lesson 2.9.)

title: 3.7 - Making Pictures with AI
text:
🛠️ Try It

3.7.3 - Watch Noise Become a Picture
Work with a partner. (In a big class, groups of 3 share one computer.)


Choose words. Press Remove some noise one step at a time. At which step can you guess the picture?
Press New noise with the same words. Play it. What changed? What stayed the same?
Keep the noise. Choose new words. Play it. What changed?




  
    Your words:
    
  
  
    Noise:
    🎲 New noise
    
  
  
    
    
      
      
        ➡️ Remove some noise
        ▶️ Play
        ↺ Back to noise
      
      
    
  
  





This shows the idea, but it cheats. This demo already has the finished picture (an emoji), and it mixes the noise away. A real image generator doesn’t have the picture. Its neural network has to guess what to remove, using what it learned from millions of pictures.

Don’t make AI pictures of classmates, teachers, or anyone real. A fake picture of a real person can hurt them, even as a joke. (More in Lesson 4.3.)

title: 3.7 - Making Pictures with AI
text:
💬 Talk About It
Is a picture made by AI art? Who should get the credit: the person who wrote the prompt, the company that made the AI, or the artists whose pictures trained it?


The noise turned into a picture when …
The same prompt made different pictures because …
An AI picture (is / isn’t) art, because …
The credit should go to … , because …

title: 3.7 - Making Pictures with AI
text:
🚀 Go Further

Work with a partner, or in a group of 3. Picture tools have a limit on how many pictures a class can make, so each pair shares turns. If your class AI tool can’t make pictures today, give your prompts to your teacher. Your teacher makes them on the projector.
A good picture prompt says what you want to see:



Part

Find one mistake in a picture. Write it down.

Small class: every pair gets 3 pictures. Big class: play “Describe It.” One student from each team sees a secret picture. The team writes a prompt from the description and makes one picture. Whose is closest?


Choose one subject, like “a bus at our school.” Write 5 prompts for it in 5 styles: photo, cartoon, pixel art, oil painting, and a style from your home country. Make the 5 pictures, or give the prompts to your teacher. Make a poster of the 5 pictures.


Write prompts for “a doctor,” “a nurse,” “a scientist,” and “a basketball player.” Your teacher makes each one 4 times. Count who the AI shows: men or women, young or old, skin colors. What do you notice? Bring your results to Lesson 4.2.

title: 3.8 - Project: Solve a Real Problem
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Your mom gets a letter from the school, in English, with a deadline. You want a job at a grocery store, and you need a résumé. You have a biology test next week. You want to sell the bracelets you make.
These are real problems. In this unit, you learned to ask good questions, keep talking, get feedback, check facts, test translations, check math, and make pictures. Now put it all together. Use AI to help solve a problem in your life.
Write 3 problems in your life or your family’s life. Big or small. Then circle the one you care about most.

title: 3.8 - Project: Solve a Real Problem
text: Reading letters in English. Finding a job. Studying for a test. Planning a meal with what is in the kitchen. Saving money for something. Learning to drive. Planning a birthday party. Helping a younger brother or sister with homework.

title: 3.8 - Project: Solve a Real Problem
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.8.1 - Choose a Good Problem
A good project problem is:

Real: you or your family really have this problem.
Small: you can finish it in about 2 class days.
Useful: you make something you’ll really use.









Problem

Your plan answers 6 questions. You write it on your sheet.

What is the problem?

What will you make? (your product)
How will AI help?
What will you check, and how?
What will you do yourself?




3.8.3 - The Rules


Use at least 3 skills from Unit 3.
Keep a prompt log: every prompt you use, and what you did with the answer.
Check what the AI tells you. Write how you checked.
Write an AI note at the end. It’s short and honest. It says what you did and what the AI did (Lesson 3.3).

This chart is the rubric. It shows how your project is graded.

title: 3.8 - Project: Solve a Real Problem
text:
🛠️ Try It

title: 4.2 - Where Bias Comes From
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In 2014, Amazon started building an AI to pick the best job applications. It learned from the applications of people Amazon had hired over 10 years. Most of them were men.
The AI learned to give lower scores to applications with the word “women’s,” like “captain of the women’s soccer team.” Nobody told it to do that. It learned it from the examples. Amazon stopped using it.
Today you find out where unfair AI comes from. Then you act out the story of a horse that fooled a whole city.
In Turkish, there’s one word for “he” and “she”: o. So “O bir doktor” can mean “He is a doctor” or “She is a doctor.”
Your teacher types these into Google Translate, from Turkish to English:
Before he presses Enter, predict: will the AI choose “he” or “she” for each one? Why?

title: 4.2 - Where Bias Comes From
text:
O bir doktor. O bir hemşire. (doctor, nurse)



Turkish didn’t say. The AI has to guess. It guesses from its training examples. If most English sentences it read said “he is a doctor” and “she is a nurse,” that’s what it predicts. The AI didn’t decide that women can’t be doctors. It copied a pattern from its data.


After people complained, Google Translate started showing both “he” and “she” for some short sentences in some languages. Longer sentences, and other tools, may still choose one.

title: 4.2 - Where Bias Comes From
text:
👥 Learn Together

4.2.1 - What Is Bias?
In AI, bias means a system is unfair to some people, or works better for some people than for others. It’s usually not on purpose. It gets in three ways:

The data copies the past. If the past was unfair, the AI learns the unfair pattern. Amazon’s AI learned from 10 years of mostly male hires. The translator learned a stereotype, “he is a doctor,” from millions of old sentences.
Some people are missing. Face programs from big companies made far more mistakes on darker-skinned women. Their training dataset had far fewer faces like theirs.
Shortcuts. The AI finds a clue that works in training, but it isn’t the real reason. This one is the strangest. Read on.




4.2.2 - Shortcuts

In Berlin, a horse named Hans seemed to do arithmetic. His owner asked, “What is 3 + 2?” Hans tapped his hoof 5 times. Crowds came to see him. Experts couldn’t find a trick.



Clever Hans and his owner, Wilhelm von Osten, in Berlin. The boards hold numbers and letters. Hans answered by tapping. (Photo from the early 1900s, public domain)


In 1907, a scientist named Oskar Pfungst tried two tests:

When the person asking did not know the answer, Hans got it wrong.
When Hans could not see the person, Hans got it wrong.

Hans couldn’t do math. He watched people’s faces and bodies. When he reached the right number, people relaxed a tiny bit, without knowing it. Hans stopped tapping. He learned a shortcut.

AI can do the same thing. In 2016, researchers made an AI to tell wolves from huskies (a dog that looks like a wolf). They chose the training pictures on purpose: every wolf was in snow. They wanted to see if people would notice the problem.





The AI learned to look at the snow, not the animal. Many people who tested it didn’t notice until the researchers showed them. Researchers now call this the “Clever Hans” problem in AI: right answers for the wrong reason.

It wasn’t a photo. A man in Chicago made it with an AI image generator, as a joke. He didn’t expect so many people to believe it.

title: 4.3 - Real or Fake?
text:
👥 Learn Together

4.3.1 - Why the Clues Stop Working
An AI fake of a real person, like the Pope picture, is called a deepfake. People used to look for clues like these:



Old clue
What happened




Hands with 6 fingers
Newer tools draw hands well.


Messy words on signs
Newer tools can write words.


Earrings that don’t match
Newer tools fix this.


Strange, blurry backgrounds
Newer tools fix this too.



Every time people find a clue, the companies fix it. So looking for clues in the picture doesn’t work for long.



4.3.2 - Check the Source, Not the Picture
Fact-checkers don’t stare at a picture. They ask where it came from. Use the four steps called SIFT:



Step
What you do




Stop
Before you share it, stop. Do you feel very angry or surprised? Be careful.


Investigate the source
Who posted it first? Are they a real news organization?


Find better coverage
Search for it. Are trusted news sources reporting it?


Trace to the original
Use a reverse image search to find the first place it appeared.






4.3.3 - Fake Voices
Fakes aren’t only pictures. AI can make fake voices, too. It can copy a voice from a short recording, maybe a video someone posted online. Scammers use voice clone calls that sound like a family member in trouble: “Mom, I need money right now!”

Choose a family safe word: a secret word that only your family knows. If someone calls in a panic asking for money, ask for the safe word. Then hang up and call the person back on their real number. Calling back is the same idea as SIFT: you check the source, not the voice.

title: 4.4 - Why AI Cheat Detectors Fail
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Some schools use “AI detectors.” A teacher puts in a student’s essay. The detector says: “87% likely written by AI.”
In 2023, researchers at Stanford University tested 7 popular detectors. They used 91 essays written by people learning English, for an English test. The detectors said 61% of them were written by AI. Almost all of them (98%) were called AI by at least one detector.
Every one of those essays was written by a person. Today you find out why detectors blame people who write in a second language, like many students in this room.
Your teacher reads 4 short paragraphs. Some were written by students in Lesson 3.3 (no names). Some were written by AI. After each one, hold up H for human or A for AI.
