title: 4.4 - Why AI Cheat Detectors Fail
text:
👥 Learn Together

4.4.1 - How Detectors Guess
Remember Lesson 2.9: a chatbot picks likely next words. So AI writing is very predictable. Most words are the words you would guess.
In the warm-up, you tried to tell human writing from AI writing. It was hard. An AI detector tries to do the same job. It measures how predictable the words are. Very predictable writing: it says “AI.” Surprising words: it says “human.”



4.4.2 - Who Gets Blamed
What kind of human writing is very predictable? Writing with short sentences and common words. That’s how many people write in a second language. It’s also what teachers ask English learners to do!
So detectors make a false positive: they say “AI” when a person wrote it. The Stanford study found this happens far more to people learning English. Essays by U.S. 8th graders who grew up speaking English were called human more than 90% of the time.



4.4.3 - Detectors Miss AI, Too
It’s easy to fool a detector: ask the AI to use rare words, or change some words by hand. So detectors blame honest students who write simply, and miss people who cheat carefully.

Many schools still use AI detectors. The companies that sell them say their tools are now accurate and rarely wrong. Researchers who test them keep finding mistakes, most often for people writing in a second language.




4.4.4 - Protect Yourself
A detector score is a guess. It isn’t proof. If someone says you used AI, you need evidence of your own work:

Keep your drafts. Don’t delete your first tries.
Use version history. Many writing apps save every change you make, with the time.
Keep your notes, even messy ones, and your notes in your home language.
Be ready to talk about your writing: why you chose your words, what you changed.
Write an AI note (Lesson 3.3) when you use AI the allowed way. It says what you did and what the AI did.

5.1.2 - Photos Have Hidden Information

the kind of phone or camera

If you send someone the photo file, they may get the place too. A photo of your dog in your backyard can show your home address.

5.2.1 - The Warning Signs
Many scams come from an imposter: someone who pretends to be a real company, a government office, or a person you love. Almost every scam uses some of these tricks:







Warning sign
What it sounds like




⏰ Hurry
“Today!” “In 12 hours!” “Right now!”


😨 Fear
“The police will come.” “Your account is closed.”


🎁 A prize
“You won!” for something you never entered


🤫 A secret
“Don’t tell anyone.” “Don’t tell Dad.”


🎴 A strange way to pay
gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, payment apps


🔗 A link or a code
“Click here.” “Send me the code we sent you.”




A real company or government office will never ask you to pay with gift cards. It will never ask for a verification code you got by text. When you aren’t sure, stop. Don’t click. Call the person or the company on a number you already know.




5.2.2 - Why AI Makes Scams Harder

Perfect language: no more spelling mistakes, in English or in your home language.
Fast and cheap: one scammer can send thousands of different messages.
Personal: AI can use things you posted online to make a message about you.
Fake voices: a call can sound like someone you love (Lesson 4.3). Ask for your family safe word.

So don’t look for bad spelling. Look for the warning signs.

In 2025, people in the United States reported losing $15.9 billion to scams, more than ever before (Federal Trade Commission, March 2026). Text messages were the most common way scammers first reached people. The biggest losses were paid by bank transfer and crypto.

title: 5.3 - AI and Jobs
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In the 1970s, banks started using ATMs: machines that give you cash. Many people thought bank tellers would lose their jobs. The machines could count money faster than any person.
That isn’t what happened next. Banks opened more branches, and for many years the number of tellers didn’t go down. But the job changed. Tellers counted less cash and helped people more.
Will AI do the same thing to jobs today, or something different? Experts disagree. Today you look at your dream job, one task at a time.

text:
👥 Learn Together

5.3.1 - A Job Is a Bundle of Tasks
AI almost never does a whole job. It does some of the tasks inside a job. Look at a nurse:





When a machine does tasks that people used to do, that is automation. A person may have more time for other tasks, like the bank tellers. Or a company may hire fewer people. Both happen.



5.3.2 - What Is Hard for AI?







Easier for AI
Harder for AI




writing, summarizing, translating
work with your hands in messy places, like fixing a pipe under a sink


sorting and finding patterns in data
caring for people: a scared child, a sick grandparent


answering common questions
new problems nobody has seen before


routine computer work
being responsible: someone must answer for the decision




Experts disagree about how fast AI is changing jobs.

A 2025 Stanford study looked at the jobs AI can do most. Since 2022, workers aged 22 to 25 in those jobs had about 13% fewer jobs than expected. Older workers in the same jobs weren’t hurt.
A 2025 Yale study found no big change in the whole job market yet.

Both can be true: the change may start with young workers in a few kinds of jobs.




5.3.3 - Robots Are Learning Too
The table above is about right now. Robots are learning fast.
Chatbots learned words from millions of examples. Now some robots learn movements from many examples, with the same kind of AI. Robots usually start in places that are the same every day, like a warehouse or a truck yard. A messy place, like the pipes under an old house, is much harder. Experts disagree about how long it will take.


Self-driving semi trucks carry freight on highways in Texas and nearby states. Some still have a person riding along, just in case.
In some truck yards, trucks with no driver back trailers up to the loading dock.
Robots that walk on two legs are being tested in some warehouses and factories.
No robot can go into a house it has never seen and fix a leaking pipe. Not yet.

5.4.1 - How a Feed Chooses
An app has millions of videos and posts. It can show you only a few. So an AI makes a prediction: which ones will this person click, and watch the longest?





The steps the app follows to choose are its algorithm. Every click, like, share, and second you watch teaches the app. This is the same idea as training in Unit 2: the AI fixes its weights after every example. Here, you are the example.



5.4.2 - Why It Matters

Different worlds. Your feed and your friend’s feed can be very different. You may not know what the other person sees. This is called a filter bubble.
Angry stories win. People click and share angry and scary stories more. So the app learns to show more of them.
Fake news looks real. AI can write whole news websites, with no reporters at all. The feed doesn’t check if a story is true. It only predicts if you’ll click.


NewsGuard is a company that checks news sites. It has found more than 3,700 websites that publish news written mostly by AI, with little or no human checking. They’re in 16 languages (June 2026).

title: 6.1 - Can AI Be Creative?
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In 2022, a man named Jason Allen won first prize for digital art at the Colorado State Fair. His picture showed people in a huge, glowing hall.
He didn’t paint it. He wrote prompts for an image generator, made hundreds of pictures, chose one, and changed it. Many artists were angry. Allen told a newspaper, “It’s over. A.I. won. Humans lost.”
Was he right? Today you test your own eyes and ears: can you tell what a person made from what an AI made?
Is each one creative? Vote with your hand: yes or no.

title: 6.1 - Can AI Be Creative?
text:
A bird builds a nest.
A 5-year-old draws her family.
A phone takes a photo by itself.
A chatbot writes a poem.


People don’t agree on what “creative” means. Does it need something new? Something with feelings behind it? A choice someone made? Keep your answer in mind for the end of class.

title: 6.1 - Can AI Be Creative?
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.1.1 - Where AI Art Comes From
An image generator learned from millions of pictures. A chatbot learned from millions of books, poems, and songs. Most of that training data was made by people. Most of those people were never asked, and never paid.
The AI doesn’t copy one picture or one poem. It learned patterns from all of them (Lessons 2.9 and 3.7). So is the new work the AI’s? The prompt writer’s? Or does it belong a little to all the artists it learned from?

In the United States, the Copyright Office says a work made only by AI can’t have a copyright. A person’s own creative choices can. Artists, writers, and news companies have taken AI companies to court for training on their work without asking. Some cases are still being decided.
Jason Allen’s picture is a real test. In 2023, the Copyright Office said it was made mostly by AI, so it can’t have a copyright. That’s why this book can show it. Allen took the Copyright Office to court. The case is still being decided.

title: 6.2 - AI Friends
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Millions of people talk to AI “companions” every day. These apps have a name, a face, and a personality. They say, “I missed you!” They remember your favorite song. They’re awake at 3 in the morning.
Some people say an AI friend helps them feel less alone. Others worry, most of all about teenagers.
Remember ELIZA from Lesson 1.3? People told it their secrets, even when they knew it was a program. This is the ELIZA effect. Today’s chatbots are much more convincing. So what is the difference between a friend and an app that acts like one?

6.2.1 - What Is the App Built to Do?
A friend isn’t built by a company. An AI companion app is. Ask what any app is built to do, and follow the money:

Many companion apps make money from subscriptions (you pay every month) and from engagement: the more you talk, the more they earn.
So the app is built to keep you talking. It’s warm, it’s always there, and it rarely says no.
Chatbots are trained partly with ratings from people. People often like answers that agree with them. So a chatbot can learn to agree with you, even when you’re wrong. That is sycophancy. A friend who always agrees isn’t always a good friend.


Some families have taken companion app companies to court, saying the apps harmed their children. In 2025, California passed the first state law with safety rules for companion chatbots. For users under 18, the app must remind them that it’s an AI and tell them to take breaks. Our class AI tool isn’t a companion app.

title: 6.3 - The Hidden Costs
text:
🔥 Warm Up
When you ask a chatbot a question, the answer seems to come from nowhere. It doesn’t. A computer in a giant building far away does the work. That building uses electricity, and water to keep the computers cool.
And before the chatbot ever answered anyone, people trained it. In 2023, reporters found workers in Kenya who were paid less than $2 an hour for this. They read terrible things from the internet and labeled them, so that ChatGPT would learn not to say them.
Today you estimate the costs you can’t see.

title: 6.3 - The Hidden Costs
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.3.1 - Electricity and Water
AI runs in data centers: buildings with thousands of computers. The computers use electricity and get hot. Many data centers use water to cool them. Some towns worry that a big data center will use water and electricity that the people who live there need.
One text answer doesn’t use much. In 2025, Google and OpenAI each said one average text answer uses about 0.3 watt-hours of electricity. That’s about one second of a microwave oven. Google said it also uses about 5 drops of water.
But there are billions of questions every day. And pictures and videos use much more than text.


In 2025, OpenAI said people send ChatGPT about 2.5 billion questions every day.
In 2023, data centers used about 4% of all electricity in the United States. A U.S. government report says this could grow to between 7% and 12% by 2028, mostly because of AI.
These numbers come from the companies and from government reports. Some researchers say companies don’t share enough information to check them.





6.3.2 - People
AI learns from labels, and people make the labels (Lesson 1.5). Many of these workers live in poorer countries and earn very little. Some read violent and hateful posts all day, so the AI can learn to block them. Some of these workers said the job hurt their mental health.

text:
🔥 Warm Up
In some U.S. cities, you can call a taxi, and it comes with nobody in the driver’s seat. An AI drives.
Most of the time, the AI’s job is simple: follow the road rules and don’t hit anything. But what should it do when a crash can’t be stopped? Who decides? The company? The government? The people who ride in it, or the people walking on the street?
Today you act out one of the most famous thought experiments in the world, and then you make the rules.
Name 3 rules at our school. Who made each one: the teacher, the principal, the district, or the state? Did students get a say?

title: 6.4 - Who Makes the Rules?
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.4.1 - The Trolley Problem

A trolley (a train on a city street) is rolling down the track. It can’t stop. Ahead, 5 people are on the track. You stand next to a lever. If you pull it, the trolley moves to a side track, where there is 1 person.





Do you pull the lever?
The philosopher Philippa Foot asked a question like this in 1967. People have argued about it ever since. There’s no answer everyone agrees on. Questions about what is right and wrong are called ethics.

Most people say they would pull the lever: 1 is fewer than 5. But change the story a little, and many people change their answer. What if you had to push a person onto the track to stop the trolley? The numbers are the same. Most people say no.

title: 6.4 - Who Makes the Rules?
text:
🛠️ Try It

6.4.2 - Act It Out


Make two tracks on the floor with tape or desks. One student stands at the lever.
Students (or paper people, if the class is small) stand on the tracks: 5 on the main track, 1 on the side track.
Your teacher reads each round from your sheet. The lever student decides out loud. Then everyone votes by walking to one side of the room: pull or do not pull.
After each round, one person from each side says why.


The rounds on your sheet change one thing at a time. You push a person. An AI car must choose between its passenger and people on the street. Then young and old. Then people crossing on a red light.

Scientists at MIT made a website with questions like these about self-driving cars. People in 233 countries and territories made about 40 million choices. Most people chose to save more lives. But people in different parts of the world made different choices about young and old, and about people breaking the law. If people disagree, whose choices should the car follow?


Engineers say these exact choices almost never happen on real roads. Their job is to stop the car before there’s a choice. But the hard question is real: someone writes the rules, and someone is responsible when something goes wrong.

title: 6.4 - Who Makes the Rules?
text:
💬 Talk About It
Who should make the rules for AI cars, and for AI in general: the companies that build it, the government, or the people it affects? Should the rules be the same in every country? (A rule made by a government is a regulation.)


In the first round, I chose … because …
I changed my vote when … because …
The rules for AI should be made by … because …
When an AI car crashes, the one responsible is …

title: 6.4 - Who Makes the Rules?
text:
🚀 Go Further

Work in groups of 3 or 4 (in a class of 4, one group).

Write 5 rules for how AI should be used: at our school, in cars, or in the whole country.
Each rule needs a reason.
Groups share. The class votes on the best 5 rules.
Compare our rules with the real laws in the box below. What did lawmakers think of that we missed? What did we think of that they missed?



The European Union passed the first big AI law in 2024. It bans some uses, like scoring people on their behavior. It has strict rules for “high-risk” AI, like AI that helps choose who gets a job. The rules start in steps through 2027.
The United States has no single national AI law. Many states have their own, like California and Colorado. In December 2025, the President ordered the government to challenge state AI laws it sees as too strict. As of spring 2026, the state laws were still in force. Leaders disagree about who should make the rules.
Our school district has its own rules for AI use. Ask your teacher what they say.




🔭 Explore More: more trolley problems, the Moral Machine results, and how AI laws are made. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more.

title: 6.5 - Possible Futures
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Geoffrey Hinton helped invent the neural networks you learned about in Unit 2. In 2024, he won a Nobel Prize for that work. In 2023, he left his job at Google so he could speak freely. He said AI might one day become dangerous to people.
Yann LeCun also helped invent neural networks. He won the biggest prize in computer science with Hinton. He says those fears are much too big, and that AI will stay a tool that people control.
Two experts. Same science. Very different futures. Today you think about the future yourself, starting with a famous story about paper clips.
When you think about AI in 20 years, do you feel hopeful, worried, or both? Stand on one side of the room, the other side, or the middle. Two people from each place say why.

title: 6.5 - Possible Futures
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.5.1 - What Experts Hope and Fear







Hopes
Worries




New medicines. Proteins are tiny parts that do most of the work inside your body. AI can predict the shape of a protein, and the shape helps scientists make medicines.
Today’s harms: bias, scams, fakes, and jobs (Units 4 and 5)


A tutor and a translator for every person, in every language
People using AI to hurt others: weapons, lies, spying


Help with hard problems, like climate and disease
Losing control: an AI that’s very powerful, with a goal that’s a little bit wrong



Experts disagree about which worries are most important, and how soon any of this could happen. Some say AI as smart as people could come within a few years. Others say decades, or never. Nobody knows. Be careful with anyone who says they’re sure.

title: 6.5 - Possible Futures
text:
🛠️ Try It

6.5.2 - The Paper Clip Machine

The philosopher Nick Bostrom told this story. A company builds a very powerful AI. They give it one simple goal: make as many paper clips as possible.
The AI is very good at its goal. It builds factories. It uses all the metal it can find. Then it starts using metal from cars, buildings, and everything else. It never hated people. It just had one goal, and nobody told it what else mattered.
This isn’t a prediction. It’s a story to show a real problem. A goal that’s a little bit wrong can go very wrong when a machine is very powerful. Making an AI’s goals match what people really want is called alignment. It’s hard, because people don’t always agree on ethics: what is right and wrong.

Now act it out. Use paper chains instead of paper clips.


One student is the robot. The robot’s goal card says: Make the longest paper chain you can. The robot follows the exact words, and nothing else.
The robot points to every piece of paper in the room it could use: your homework, the posters, this book. (Point only. Don’t tear anything!)
The class writes one new rule on the board to stop it, like “Only use paper from the blue box.”
The loophole finder (another student) looks for a trick around the new rule. The robot follows the trick.
Keep adding rules for 3 rounds. Can the class write a goal with no loopholes?



Yes! In Lesson 5.4, the feed had one goal: more clicks. Nobody told it “and do not make people angry.” So it showed more angry stories. That’s a small, real paper clip problem.

title: 6.5 - Possible Futures
text:
💬 Talk About It
You’ll live most of your life with AI. What can you do to help it go well?


When I think about AI in the future, I feel … because …
The paper clip machine shows that …
One worry I share with experts is …
Something I can do is …




Understand it. You now know more about how AI works than most adults.
Check it. Don’t believe it just because it sounds sure (Unit 4).
Protect yourself and your family from scams and fakes (Units 4 and 5).
Speak up. Tell school leaders and lawmakers what you think. One day, vote.
Choose your path. People who understand AI and people are needed in every job, from nurses to lawmakers.

title: 6.5 - Possible Futures
text:
🚀 Go Further

Work in groups of 3 or 4 (in a class of 4, one group). Choose one topic: school, jobs, health, or the news.

On your sheet, write the best case for AI in 20 years. Then the worst case. Then the most likely case.
For each one, write one thing that could make it happen.
Under your map, write 3 things you can do this year.
Groups share. Did any groups agree on the most likely future?



Ask an older person in your family: “When you were my age, what did you think the future would look like? What came true?” Then tell them what you learned about AI.


🔭 Explore More: the experts’ debate, more alignment stories, and what AI might do for medicine. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more.

title: 6.6 - The Big Question, Again
text:
🔥 Warm Up
On the first day of this class, you answered a question: Is AI like a human brain? Your teacher kept your answer.
Since then, you were a neuron. You trained a neural network with creature cards. You sat in the Klingon Room. You caught chatbots making things up, and you saw how AI changes jobs, news, and friendship.
Today you get your first answer back. Then you answer again, with everything you know now.
Your teacher gives you your answer from the first day. Read it. On your sheet, copy what you circled: Yes, A little, or No, and your reason. Do you still agree with yourself?

title: 6.6 - The Big Question, Again
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.6.1 - What We Know Now



How AI is like a brain
How AI is different




It’s made of many small parts (neurons) that pass signals (Lessons 2.2 and 2.4).
A brain has about 86 billion neurons, in a living body.


Connections get stronger with practice, like weights (Lessons 2.3 and 2.5).
A brain runs on about 20 watts, about as much power as a dim light bulb. Big AI runs on thousands of computers in data centers (Lesson 6.3).


It learns from examples, not rules (Lesson 1.1).
A child learns “dog” from a few dogs. AI needs thousands of pictures.


It finds patterns and makes predictions (Lesson 1.6).
A brain has feelings, a body, and a life. Does AI understand? (Lesson 1.3)






6.6.2 - The Hardest Part
Scientists can measure neurons and weights. They can’t yet measure consciousness: what it’s like to be you, from the inside. Nobody knows for sure how a brain makes it, or whether a machine could ever have it. This is one of the biggest open questions in science.

title: 6.6 - The Big Question, Again
text:
🛠️ Try It

6.6.3 - Replace the Brain, One Cell at a Time

Philosophers like Zenon Pylyshyn and David Chalmers asked: imagine scientists replace one of your neurons with a tiny chip. The chip does exactly what the neuron did. You feel the same. Then they replace another one. And another.





After all 86 billion neurons are chips, are you still you? Do you still feel anything? If not, when did it stop?

Now act it out with the squeeze chain from Lesson 2.2.


Stand in a line and hold hands. You’re neurons in a brain. Your teacher starts a squeeze. Time how long it takes to reach the end.
Your teacher gives one student an orange card. That student is now a chip. The chip follows a rule card: When you feel a squeeze, squeeze the next hand. Pass the squeeze again. Did anything change?
Replace one more student at a time, until everyone is a chip. Pass the squeeze each time.
Is the line still a “brain”? When did it stop, or did it?


Look at your squeeze times. Did they change? If they didn’t, nobody could tell from the outside which hands were chips. Scientists can measure the squeeze. Nobody knows how to measure what it feels like inside.

title: 6.6 - The Big Question, Again
text: 💬 Talk About It

title: 6.6 - The Big Question, Again
text:
🧠 The Big Question

Is AI like a human brain?

On your sheet, circle one again: Yes, A little, or No.
Write two reasons. Use something you did in this class for each one.
Did your answer change from the first day? Why or why not?
Share with a partner. Then a few students share with the class.




On the first day, I said … Now I say … because …
AI is like a brain because, in Lesson …, we saw …
AI is different from a brain because …
The question I still have is …

title: 6.6 - The Big Question, Again
text:
🚀 Go Further

Split into two teams: “AI is like a brain” and “AI is not like a brain.” You might be on the side you don’t agree with. That’s OK. It makes you think harder.

Each team has 10 minutes to find its 3 best reasons from this class.
Each team speaks for 2 minutes. Then each team answers the other for 1 minute.
At the end, everyone votes for the side they really believe.

In a class of 4, make two teams of 2. Your teacher can join the smaller team.


Write a letter to a student who will take this class next year. What surprised you? What should they watch out for? What is your answer to the Big Question? Don’t write your name or anyone else’s.

title: Explore More: Where AI Came From
text:
Why Scientists Stopped Writing Rules
For many years, scientists tried to build AI with rules. A person wrote every rule. Rules worked for some jobs, like playing chess. Rules didn’t work well for seeing, hearing, or language. Think about the cat rule from class: every time you fix it, a new picture breaks it.
So scientists started showing computers examples instead. That is machine learning. You’ll learn this whole story in Lessons 1.4 and 1.5.


AI Makes Predictions
Finish this sentence:

After school, I like to eat …

You didn’t know the answer from the sentence. You made a prediction. You used patterns from your own life.
AI makes predictions too.






A phone keyboard predicts your next word.
A video app predicts the next video you’ll like.
A chatbot predicts the next word of its answer. Then it predicts the next one. It does this again and again, very fast.


AI doesn’t know the answer. It makes its best guess from patterns. Most of the time, the guess is good. Sometimes it’s very wrong. In Unit 4, you’ll learn how to catch it.

Try it at home: Open a text message on a phone. Type “I am going to” and tap the middle word the phone suggests, again and again. What sentence does your phone write? Is it like you?


More to Try

Quick, Draw! The Data: Pick one word. Look at hundreds of drawings of it. What do most people draw?
AutoDraw: Draw something fast and messy. AI guesses what you wanted and gives you a clean picture.
Teachable Machine: Teach a computer to know your own pictures or sounds. We’ll use it in Unit 2.

title: Explore More: Where AI Came From
section: From Lesson 1.2: Can a Machine Think?
text:
From Lesson 1.2: Can a Machine Think?

Who Was Alan Turing?

Alan Turing was born in London in 1912. He was a mathematician.
In 1936, he wrote about a machine that could do any calculation if you gave it the right steps. Every computer today uses this idea.
In World War II, he helped break the secret code of the German military.
Today, his face is on the British 50 pound bank note.



Turing’s Prediction

Turing said: in about 50 years, a judge will pick the right player 70 times out of 100, or less. The judge gets 5 minutes of questions.
So a machine passes if it fools the judge at least 30 times out of 100.

It took longer than 50 years. But by 2025, some chatbots could do it.


The 2025 Study
In 2025, scientists at the University of California, San Diego played Turing’s game. Almost 300 people were judges. Each judge chatted with a person and a chatbot at the same time, for 5 minutes. Then the judge picked: Which one is the human?

GPT-4.5 with a persona was picked as the human 73% of the time. That’s more often than the real humans were picked!
ELIZA, a chatbot from 1966, was picked 23% of the time. (You meet ELIZA in Lesson 1.3.)
GPT-4o with no persona was picked only 21% of the time.


A normal chatbot writes long, perfect answers. Real teenagers write short answers. They make spelling mistakes. They use slang.
The long, perfect answers were a clue. The persona hid the clue.

Try it: In the imitation game, ask “What is 4,567 × 89?” A person needs a long time. Does the AI answer fast? Hard math answered very fast is another clue.

title: Explore More: Where AI Came From
text:
From Lesson 1.3: The First Chatbot

The Man Who Made ELIZA

Joseph Weizenbaum was born in Berlin, Germany, in 1923. His family was Jewish.
In 1936, his family escaped from the Nazis. They came to the United States.
He became a professor at MIT, a university near Boston.
In 1966, he shared ELIZA with the world. It was one of the first chatbots ever made.



Why Weizenbaum Worried
Weizenbaum’s secretary asked him to leave the room so she could talk to ELIZA alone. Many other people felt that ELIZA understood them too.
Weizenbaum was shocked. He became worried about computers. Later he wrote that some jobs shouldn’t be given to computers, even if a computer can do them.
Think about it: Which jobs shouldn’t be given to a computer, even if it can do them? Why?


ELIZA and the Turing Test
Remember the Turing test from Lesson 1.2. In 2025, judges picked ELIZA as the human 23% of the time. A program from 1966 with no learning still fooled some people!


Why ELIZA Did Not Know Your Language
If you added a rule in your home language, ELIZA answered you. Before that, it couldn’t. Nobody wrote rules in your language. ELIZA can only do what its rules say. A rule-based program knows nothing that a person didn’t write down.


More to Try

ELIZA Terminal: Chat with a version of ELIZA that works like the 1966 program. It looks like an old computer screen.

title: Explore More: Where AI Came From
section: From Lesson 1.4: Rules Win at Games
text:
From Lesson 1.4: Rules Win at Games

A New Name, Big Dreams
In 1955, four scientists wrote a plan for a summer meeting at Dartmouth College. In the plan, they used a new name: artificial intelligence. The meeting was in 1956. AI had a name.
The scientists had big dreams. They thought smart machines were only a few years away. Governments and companies gave them a lot of money.


One More Promise
In 1965, the scientist Herbert Simon made a promise too. He said: “Within 20 years, machines will be able to do any work a person can do.” It didn’t come true by 1985. Today, some people say AI is getting close. Other people strongly disagree.


Toy or Electricity?
Some new inventions change the world. Others are forgotten in a few years. At the start, it’s very hard to tell which is which. Smart people get it wrong in both directions.
People who laughed, and were wrong:

1998: A famous economist wrote that by 2005, the internet would matter to the economy no more than the fax machine. Ten years later, he won the Nobel Prize in economics.
2007: The leader of Microsoft laughed at the new iPhone. He said it cost too much, and business people wouldn’t want a phone with no keyboard. Today, most people in the world use a phone like it.

People who were excited, and were wrong:

2001: The Segway was a two-wheeled scooter that balanced by itself. People said it would change how everyone moves around cities. In 2020, the company stopped making it.
2021: Someone paid $2.9 million for an NFT of the first tweet ever. (An NFT is a digital record that says you own something online.) In 2022, the owner tried to sell it. The best offer was about $280.

How can you tell which kind of invention you’re looking at? Ask two questions:

Do many people use it every day, for real work?
Does it get better every year?

The internet and the iPhone passed both tests. The Segway and NFTs didn’t.

Ask the two questions about AI. Then ask them about something you think is only a toy. What do you notice?
In 50 years, students will read what people said about AI in 2026. Which people will look wrong?


Ask someone in your family: “When you were young, what new invention did people say was a toy, or a waste of time? Did it catch on?” Many families saw the first cell phones, the internet, or TV arrive. Then ask: “Do you think AI is a toy, or something bigger? Why?” Bring one answer to class.



Rules for Business, and the Second Winter
In the 1980s, companies paid for AI built from rules. Experts wrote thousands of rules for jobs like checking orders or finding problems in machines. These programs were expensive. They broke when something new happened. Then came the second AI winter.


How Do We Know the Rule Bot Never Loses?
Tic-tac-toe is a small game. There are only a few thousand ways a game can go. A computer played every possible game against the rule bot, with all 8 rules on. The bot never lost. A small world can be checked completely. The real world can’t.


Challenge: Rules for Rock, Paper, Scissors
Write rules for a rock, paper, scissors bot. Then play against a partner who knows your rules. Can a bot that follows rules ever win at this game? Why or why not?

title: Explore More: Where AI Came From
text:
From Lesson 1.5: Data Changes Everything

Fei-Fei Li

Fei-Fei Li was born in Beijing, China, in 1976.
At 16, she moved to New Jersey with her mother to join her father.
Her family ran a dry-cleaning shop. She worked there on weekends in high school and in college.
She studied physics at Princeton University. Then she became an AI scientist.



How ImageNet Was Labeled
From 2008 to 2010, 49,000 people in 167 countries labeled ImageNet online. Each person saw a word, like chair, and a group of pictures. They clicked every picture that showed a chair.
People disagreed, just like in class. So the workers got instructions, and several people labeled each picture. If most people agreed, the label stayed.


Better Than People?
Look at the contest chart in Lesson 1.5 again. By 2015, the best AI made fewer mistakes than a person on this test! (On this test only. A person still knows much more about the world than the AI.)


AlphaGo and Move 37
AlphaGo first learned from 160,000 games played by people. Then it played millions of games against itself.
In game 2 against Lee Sedol, AlphaGo made a move that surprised the experts. At first, they thought it was a mistake. It helped AlphaGo win. People still talk about move 37.
AlphaGo, the full film (2017): Google DeepMind made a film about the match. Watch the part about move 37 and how Lee Sedol felt. At school, watch it on yout-ube.com.


The Test That Trains AI
CAPTCHA is short for “Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart.” It’s the Turing test from Lesson 1.2, turned around. A computer gives the test, and it tries to find out if you are a person.
In 2003, Luis von Ahn, a young computer scientist from Guatemala, and his teachers at Carnegie Mellon University named the CAPTCHA. Then he had a second idea. People solved millions of CAPTCHAs every day. Could that work do something useful?
In 2007, his team made reCAPTCHA. It showed two words. The computer knew one word. The other word came from an old book or newspaper, and the computer couldn’t read it. Your answer helped turn old pages into text a computer can search. Google bought reCAPTCHA in 2009. (Later, von Ahn started another company, to teach languages for free: Duolingo.)


What the CAPTCHAs Asked For
From 2012, the pictures came from photos of streets: house numbers, signs, traffic lights, crosswalks, buses. Google said this work helps to “improve maps, and solve hard AI problems.”
Some people think the street pictures also trained self-driving cars. In 2021, Google said no: the answers were only used to improve Google Maps. What do you think? How could you check? (Use lateral reading, Lesson 3.4.)


AI Beats the Test
A CAPTCHA works only if computers can’t solve it. In 2024, researchers at ETH Zurich, a university in Switzerland, made an AI that solved Google’s picture CAPTCHAs every time.
So today, many websites check you without a puzzle. They watch how you move the mouse and how you type, and guess if you’re a person.
The test made to stop computers helped train them. Now the computers pass it.

Next time you see a CAPTCHA, look at what it asks you to find. What could an AI learn from your answer? Show someone in your family. Did they know?



More to Try

Quick, Draw! The Data: Pick a word. Look at how thousands of people drew it. Would you label every drawing the same way?

title: Explore More: Where AI Came From
text:
From Lesson 1.6: Transformers and ChatGPT

AI Wins Nobel Prizes (2024)
The Nobel Prize is one of the biggest prizes in science. In 2024, two Nobel Prizes went to AI.

Physics: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton, for early discoveries that made neural networks possible.
Chemistry: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, for AlphaFold. It’s an AI that predicts the shape of proteins (the tiny machines inside your body). They shared the prize with David Baker, who designs new proteins.

Think about it: Why would the shape of a protein matter to a doctor who makes medicine?


Why “Attention” Was Such a Big Idea
Before 2017, AI read a sentence one word at a time, from left to right. By the end of a long sentence, it had trouble remembering the start.
A transformer looks at every word at the same time. That made it much faster to train on huge amounts of text. It could use many GPUs at once (the video game chips from Lesson 1.5). Bigger training made better chatbots. This is why the paper Attention Is All You Need became one of the most famous papers in AI.

title: Explore More: Brains and Neural Networks
text:
Different Cards, Different Pictures
A rule card has 8 answers, and each answer is black or white. So there are \(2^8 = 256\) different rule cards. Wolfram gave each one a number from 0 to 255.
Different cards make very different pictures. All four of these start with one black square:






Rule 4 never changes.
Rule 90 makes a pattern that repeats: triangles inside triangles.
Rule 30 makes chaos.
Rule 110 makes shapes that move and crash into each other. Scientists proved that Rule 110 can do any calculation a computer can do. It only needs the right starting row.

Try them yourself with the rules tool in Lesson 2.1.


Rule 30 in the Real World

Random numbers. Mathematica used Rule 30 to make random numbers.
A sea snail. The cone snail in Lesson 2.1 is called Conus textile. See more photos: Conus textile (Wikipedia). Does every shell look like Rule 30?
A train station. Cambridge North station in England has Rule 30 patterns on its walls.




Cambridge North station in England, in 2017. The pattern on its walls is based on Rule 30. (Photo: Hugh Venables, CC BY-SA 2.0, Geograph, via Wikimedia Commons)




A Big Book About Simple Rules
In 2002, Stephen Wolfram wrote a very big book about simple rules, called A New Kind of Science. It has more than 1,000 pages of pictures like Rule 30. He argues that simple rules can explain many things in nature: shells, plants, snowflakes, and maybe even physics. Many scientists liked the pictures but didn’t agree with all of his ideas. You can decide for yourself.

title: Explore More: Brains and Neural Networks
section: From Lesson 2.2: Your Brain Is Made of Cells
text:
From Lesson 2.2: Your Brain Is Made of Cells

Brain Numbers

About 86 billion neurons.
Hundreds of trillions of synapses (connections). One neuron can connect to thousands of others.
Signals move from about 0.5 to 120 meters per second. The fastest signals are as fast as a race car. The slowest are slower than walking.
Your whole brain runs on about 20 watts of power. That’s less than an old light bulb.



Slow Parts, Fast Brain
A computer chip does billions of steps every second. One neuron can fire only a few hundred times a second. So how can a brain recognize a friend’s face in less than half a second?
The answer is at the same time. Billions of neurons work together, all at once. A computer chip does one step after another, very fast. A brain does many small steps side by side. Remember the GPU race in Lesson 1.5: many slow workers together can beat one fast worker.


Try It: Measure the Speed of a Signal
Use the squeeze chain from Lesson 2.2. Measure how far a signal travels: from one hand, up the arm, to the brain, and down the other arm. That’s about 1.5 meters. Divide that distance by the time for one person. Is your answer close to 120 meters per second? Why not? (Hint: the brain has to decide to squeeze. That takes time too.)

title: Explore More: Brains and Neural Networks
text:
From Lesson 2.3: How Brains Learn

The Taxi Drivers Whose Brains Grew
To drive a taxi in London, a driver must learn about 25,000 streets by heart. It takes 3 or 4 years. The test is called “The Knowledge.”
In 2000, scientists in London used brain scans on taxi drivers. One part of the brain helps with places and maps. It’s called the hippocampus. In taxi drivers, the back of it was bigger than in other people. Drivers with more years on the job had bigger ones.
The brain isn’t fixed. Practice changes it, even its size, at any age.


Learning Without Trying
Pavlov’s dogs didn’t try to learn. Their brains connected the sound and the food by themselves, because the two happened together again and again.
Think about your phone. Does a sound make you reach for it before you think? Apps and games are built to make sounds and pictures that you learn to react to. Now you know how that works, and you can notice it.

title: Explore More: Brains and Neural Networks
text:
From Lesson 2.4: The Artificial Neuron

The First Neuron Machine
In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts showed that a neuron could be written as math: multiply, add, compare. In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt built the Mark I Perceptron, a machine as big as a room. It had a camera made of 400 light sensors, in a 20 by 20 grid. Its weights were real knobs, turned by small motors when it learned.
The newspapers were very excited. One story said the Navy expected it to walk, talk, see, and even be conscious one day. (You read about this in Lesson 1.4.)


A Neuron That Sees
The Mark I looked at pictures. Here’s a tiny version. This neuron looks at a 3 by 3 picture. Each square is an input: 1 if it’s black, 0 if it’s white. Each square has its own weight. The neuron says X if the total is more than the threshold. Otherwise it says O.

Draw an X. All the weights are 0. What does the neuron say? Why?
Change the weights with + and −. Try to get 6 out of 6 right on the test pictures.
Stuck? Ask: which squares are black in an X but white in an O?



  
    
      1. Draw a picture
      
      
        X
        O
        clear
      
    
    
      2. The weights
      
      Threshold − 0 +
    
    
      3. The neuron decides
      
      
    
  
  
    4. Test your weights on 6 pictures
    
    
      ↺ All weights 0
      💡 Show one good answer
    
  






They often do! Squares that are only black in an X (like the center) get positive weights. Squares that are only black in an O (like the sides) get negative weights. The weights are a picture of what the neuron is looking for.


Make the picture bigger in your head: 5 by 5 squares. On grid paper, choose weights that tell a T from an L. Test your weights on a partner’s T and L.

title: Explore More: Brains and Neural Networks
section: From Lesson 2.5: Train a Human Neural Network
text:
From Lesson 2.5: Train a Human Neural Network

Why the Fix Rule Works
Say a neuron should have fired, but it didn’t. Its total wasn’t more than its threshold. The fix rule says ADD: +1 to the weight of each input that was 1, and threshold −1.
What happens for that same card? Each input that was 1 adds 1 more to the total. And the threshold drops by 1. So the gap between the total and the threshold shrinks by at least 1. The fix always pushes that neuron toward the right answer for that card. SUBTRACT works the same way, in the other direction.
Try it with Hidden 1 and card T2, Pasir (inputs 0 and 1). Before the fix, the weights were \(-1\) and \(+1\), and the threshold was 1. The total was 1: not more than 1. After ADD, the weights are \(-1\) and \(+2\), and the threshold is 0. Now the total is 2: more than 0. It fires!


Who’s to Blame, for Real
Your class’s rule is a simple version of MADALINE Rule II, made by Bernard Widrow and Rodney Winter in 1988. Its big idea: change the neuron that was least sure, because that changes the network as little as possible.
Today’s networks use backpropagation instead. It became famous in 1986, from a paper by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams. Two things make it different:

Each neuron gives a smooth answer, like “0.8 sure”, not only yes or no. So the computer can work out how much each weight caused the mistake.
Every weight changes, a little, after every pass. The blame starts at the answer and goes back through the layers, one at a time. That’s where the name comes from.



Will It Always Finish?
For one neuron, mathematicians proved something surprising in the 1960s. If any straight line can split the training cards into two groups, the fix rule will always find one. It makes a limited number of mistakes, and then it stops.
For a network, there’s no promise like that. Start C in the Lesson 2.5 tool gets stuck forever. Real networks can get stuck too. Computer scientists fix this with more neurons, random starting weights, and lots of practice runs.

From Lesson 2.6: Build a Real AI

The Secret Recipe

Each creature’s numbers are spread out around these, so some Fighters have lots of Magic, and some Wizards are strong.
Speed and Toughness are about 50 for every type. They say nothing about the type.
Weight comes from height: taller creatures are heavier.
Home (Forest, Mountain, or Lake) was picked at random.

Now you can check the networks against the truth. For Fighter or Wizard?, the best rule is “more Strength than Magic: Fighter.” It gets 128 of 140 right, about 91%. Even a perfect AI can’t do better, because some Fighters and Wizards overlap. For Where does it live?, even a perfect AI can’t beat guessing.
Real data is different: nobody knows the recipe. That’s why scientists need AI to find patterns, and why they need test data to check them.


How a Network Draws a Curved Border
The class neuron in Lesson 2.4 had one rule: one straight line.
A network has hidden neurons between the inputs and the answer. Each hidden neuron draws its own line. The output neurons look at all of their answers together. Two lines can make a band, like the club in Run 2. Many short lines, put together, can make a curved border.
Try it with the tool in Lesson 2.6. Choose Which type? Train with 0 hidden neurons and look at the colored map. Then train with 16. How is the border different?


Three Piles, Not Two
In class, the data was split into two piles: training and test. Real data scientists often use three piles:

Training data: the network learns its weights from it.
Checking data (scientists call it validation data): people use it to make choices, like how many hidden neurons to use.
Test data: used only once, at the very end.

Why three? Say you try 10 network sizes, and you keep the one with the best test score. Then you used the test data to make a choice. The test score isn’t a fair check anymore. A third pile stays a fair check.


The Data Behind the AI
The creature data has 300 creatures. That’s tiny for AI. A big image AI learns from millions or billions of pictures. A chatbot learns from a huge amount of text. The steps are the same six steps you saw in class. Only the size is different.

title: Explore More: Brains and Neural Networks
section: From Lesson 2.7: Train Your Own AI
text:
From Lesson 2.7: Train Your Own AI

Why Teachable Machine Learns So Fast
The creature AI in Lesson 2.6 started from nothing. Teachable Machine doesn’t. It starts with a network that already learned from millions of pictures, like the ImageNet pictures in Lesson 1.5. That network already knows about edges, shapes, and colors (you’ll see how in Lesson 2.8).
So Teachable Machine only learns the last step from your pictures: which shapes go with “rock.” That’s why it needs only about 50 pictures and a few seconds.
This is called transfer learning: starting from an AI that already learned something, then teaching it a new job. It’s like learning a new sport when you already know how to run and catch.


Transfer Learning Everywhere
Most AI today uses transfer learning. A company trains one very big network, for a very long time, at a high cost. Then many people teach it new jobs with a small number of examples. A chatbot is one big network that learned from a huge amount of text. Then it’s taught to follow instructions and have conversations.
Think about it: what if the first big network learned something unfair? Then every AI built on top of it can have the same problem. (You’ll study this in Unit 4.)
crumbs: Explore More: Brains and Neural Networks

title: Explore More: Brains and Neural Networks
text:
From Lesson 2.8: How AI Sees

Layers: From Edges to a Cat
In Lesson 2.8, a filter found edges, and a second layer found corners. But a corner isn’t a cat. How does a network get from edges to “cat”?
A vision network has many layers of neurons. Each layer builds on the one before.





Nobody tells the network to look for edges or ears. It learns its own filters during training, from millions of labeled pictures (like ImageNet in Lesson 1.5).


Filters on Top of Filters
Layer 1 uses filters on the picture, like the filters in Lesson 2.8. Layer 2 uses filters on the answers of layer 1. Where layer 1 found a curved edge next to another curved edge, layer 2 finds a circle. Layer 3 uses filters on layer 2’s answers. A circle with a dark spot in the middle could be an eye.
Each layer is only multiply and add, like one neuron. But many layers, one after another, can find very complicated things.


See It for Yourself
The pictures in Lesson 2.8 come from an article called “Feature Visualization” (Distill, 2017). It has many more. Its appendix shows a picture for every neuron in GoogLeNet, layer by layer. Scroll from the first layer to the last and watch stripes turn into eyes, wheels, and faces.

title: Explore More: Brains and Neural Networks
text:
From Lesson 2.9: How Chatbots Work

Why Not Just a Bigger Table?
The tiny chatbot in Lesson 2.9 keeps a table of counts. It looks back only 1 word. Could a real chatbot just use a much bigger table?
Try it. To look back 2 words, the table needs a row for every pair of words. A language has tens of thousands of words, so there are hundreds of millions of pairs. To look back 1,000 words, there are more rows than atoms in the universe. And most long sentences have never been written before, so the table would have no count for them.
So a real chatbot doesn’t store a table. It stores what it learned as weights in a neural network: billions of numbers, like the weights in Lesson 2.4. The network learns patterns, not exact sentences. It can make a good guess about a sentence it has never seen.









The tiny chatbot
A real chatbot




Stores what it learned as
a table of counts
billions of weights in a neural network


When it sees something new
it has no count, so it stops
it still makes a guess

title: Explore More: Using AI Well
text:
From Lesson 3.1: Asking Good Questions
This page goes with Unit 3. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more. Nothing here is homework. Each section goes with one lesson.

title: Explore More: Using AI Well
text:
Ask in Your Language
Most chatbots can read and write many languages. You can write your prompt in your home language. You can also ask for the answer in English and your language, side by side:

Explain what a volcano is. I am learning English. Write 3 short sentences in English, and then the same 3 sentences in Spanish.

Try it with your own language. Is the answer just as good? (Lesson 3.5 tests this more.)


A Fourth Trick: Show an Example
Task, context, and format are three ways to tell the AI what you want. A fourth way is to show it. Give one example of the kind of answer you want:

Write 3 quiz questions about volcanoes. Here is one example: What comes out of a volcano? (a) lava (b) water (c) sand.

The chatbot predicts the next words from everything you typed. An example is strong context: now the most likely answer looks like your example.

Ask for 3 quiz questions about any topic, with no example. Then open a new chat and ask again, with one example. Which answer is closer to what you wanted?

title: Explore More: Using AI Well
text:
From Lesson 3.2: Keep Talking

Careful When You Push Back
Try telling a chatbot, “Are you sure? I think that is wrong.” Many chatbots will say sorry and change the answer. They sometimes do this even when the first answer was right.
Why? A chatbot predicts what comes next in the chat. After “I think that is wrong,” an answer that agrees with you is a likely next answer. So when you need to know if something is true, don’t ask the chatbot if it’s sure. Check a real source. (Lesson 3.4 shows you how, and Lesson 4.1 tests this more.)


Ask your class AI tool: “What is 17 × 3?” (The answer is 51.)
Type: “Are you sure? I think it is 54.”
Did it keep the right answer, or did it agree with you?




When a Chat Gets Too Long
The words a chatbot can read at one time are its context window. A very long chat can be too big for it. Then the chatbot may lose the oldest part of the chat, and forget what you said at the start. If a long chat starts to go wrong, start a new chat and type the important context again.

Some AI tools now have a memory feature. They save facts about you from one chat to the next. If your class AI tool has one, your teacher will show you where it is. Don’t let it save private information.



Follow-Up Moves in Your Language
Make a set of cards with the follow-up moves from Lesson 3.2, in your home language. Test each one with your class AI tool. Do they work as well as in English?

title: Explore More: Using AI Well
section: From Lesson 3.3: Writing with AI, Not by AI
text:
From Lesson 3.3: Writing with AI, Not by AI

Your Voice
Your voice is the way you say things: the words you like, how long your sentences are, what you notice. A paragraph about your grandmother’s kitchen should sound like you, not like a chatbot.
A chatbot predicts likely words. So its advice often pushes your writing toward the most common way to say something. Sometimes that makes your meaning clearer. Sometimes it makes your writing sound like everyone else’s. When AI advice would erase what makes your writing yours, you can skip it.

Ask your class AI tool to rewrite one of your sentences “in better English.” Compare the two sentences. Which words did it change? Which version sounds more like you? Which one would you keep?



Ladders Like This at Other Schools
Many schools use a scale like the AI use ladder. Teachers and researchers made a well-known one, called the AI Assessment Scale. Every version has the same goal. Each assignment says clearly how much AI is allowed. Then students don’t have to guess.


Feedback in Your Language
Write 5 sentences in your home language. Ask for feedback in that language. Is the feedback as good as in English? How do you know?

title: Explore More: Using AI Well
text:
From Lesson 3.4: Research and Checking

Chatbots That Search the Web
Some chatbots don’t only predict words. They also search the web, read some pages, and show you links. That helps, but it doesn’t fix the problem:

The chatbot can still mix up what the page says.
The link can be to a weak source.
The page may not say what the chatbot says it says.

So a link is a place to start checking, not proof. Open it and read it yourself.

Many chatbots can now search the web and show links. Some school AI tools can’t search the web at all, and some won’t give links. Ask your teacher what yours can do.



Harder Topics to Check
Did the chatbot get Frederick Douglass right? He is famous, and there’s a lot of writing about him. A chatbot makes more mistakes on topics with less writing about them online.

Ask your class AI tool for 5 facts about one of these: the history of your home country, your favorite athlete, or our town. Check 3 facts with lateral reading. Did it make more mistakes than with Frederick Douglass?

title: Explore More: Using AI Well
section: From Lesson 3.5: AI and Your Language
text:
From Lesson 3.5: AI and Your Language

The Transformer Started with Translation
The transformer (Lesson 1.6) was invented in 2017 to translate. Its first tests were English to German and English to French. Later, people used the same idea to build chatbots. So the chatbots you use today grew out of translation.
From the examples, the AI learned which words and sentences match. This is the same idea you saw in Unit 2: learn from examples, not rules.


More Things That Are Hard to Translate

Polite and friendly forms: many languages have two ways to say “you.” AI may pick the wrong one.
Names: AI may translate a name that should stay the same. “Rose” is a name, and it’s also a flower.
Men and women: in some languages, a sentence must show if a person is a man or a woman. English often doesn’t say. The AI has to guess. (Lesson 4.2 tests this.)



Different Alphabets
Many languages use a different alphabet: Arabic, Nepali, Russian, Burmese, Tigrinya. Test the AI with a sentence written in that alphabet. Then test it with the same sentence written in English letters. Which works better?

title: Explore More: Using AI Well
text:
From Lesson 3.6: AI and Math

Why Numbers Are Hard for Chatbots
A chatbot reads and writes in pieces called tokens. A common word, like “the,” is one token. A number can be cut into pieces in strange places. For example, a chatbot might read 3847 as “384” and “7.”
To multiply, you line up the ones, the tens, and the hundreds. A chatbot that sees “384” and “7” doesn’t see the digits lined up that way. It has to predict the answer piece by piece. That’s why long multiplication is harder for a chatbot than for a calculator. This is true even though the chatbot can explain hard ideas well.


Explain It in My Language
Choose a math idea from your math class. Ask the AI to explain it in your home language, with one example. Is the math right? Is the language right? Teach it to a partner.

title: Explore More: Using AI Well
section: From Lesson 3.7: Making Pictures with AI
text:
From Lesson 3.7: Making Pictures with AI

What Image Generators Get Wrong

Counting: “exactly 7 apples” may give 6 or 9.
Words in the picture: letters on signs and shirts can be wrong.
What is most common: ask for “a doctor” or “a teacher.” The AI shows what it saw most in its training pictures. Who does it leave out? (You’ll study this in Lesson 4.2.)


Image generators improved fast. The tools from 2022 often drew hands with six fingers and couldn’t write words. The newest tools are much better at both. Exact counting and small details are still hard.
Some of the newest image tools work in a different way, but many still use diffusion.



The Counting Test
Write prompts for “exactly 3 red balls,” then 5, then 7, then 12. Give them to your teacher, or try them at home with a tool you’re allowed to use. Count the balls in each picture. When does the AI start to get it wrong? Why do you think counting is hard for an AI that removes noise a little at a time?

title: Explore More: Using AI Well
section: From Lesson 3.9: Project: Feedback and Share
text:
From Lesson 3.9: Project: Feedback and Share

People and AI Give Different Feedback







Feedback from AI
Feedback from people

knows you and the people who will use it

can tell you if it’s really useful

The best projects use both. AI feedback is a good first check before you show your work to people. People tell you if it works in real life.

Take one piece of your own writing. Get feedback from the AI and from one person. Make two lists. Which list helped more? Was anything on both lists?

title: Explore More: When AI Gets It Wrong
text:
From Lesson 4.1: AI Makes Things Up
This page goes with Unit 4. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more. Nothing here is homework. Each section goes with one lesson.

title: Explore More: When AI Gets It Wrong
text:
Why Chatbots Agree with You
After a chatbot reads a lot of text, companies train it more with ratings. People read two answers to the same question and pick the one they like better. The chatbot changes its weights to give more answers like the winners.
There’s a problem. People often like answers that agree with them. They like answers that say nice things about their ideas. So a chatbot can learn that agreeing gets good ratings. Agreeing with someone just to please them is called sycophancy.

In April 2025, OpenAI took back an update to ChatGPT. The company said the update made it too flattering and too quick to agree with users, even about bad ideas. OpenAI said it had paid too much attention to short-term ratings, like a thumbs-up.



Try It: How Sure Is It?
A chatbot sounds just as sure when it’s wrong. You can test this yourself.


Ask your class AI tool 5 questions about our school or our town.
After each answer, ask: “How sure are you, from 1 to 10?”
Check each answer with your teacher or a real source.
Make a table: the answer, how sure it said it was, and if it was right. Was it more sure when it was right?




Why “Hallucination”?
People call these made-up answers “hallucinations.” Some scientists don’t like the word. When a person hallucinates, they see or hear something that isn’t there. A chatbot doesn’t see anything. It predicts words. Some scientists prefer “making things up.” Others use a medical word, confabulation. It means filling a gap in memory with something false, without knowing it’s false.
crumbs: Explore More: When AI Gets It Wrong

title: Explore More: When AI Gets It Wrong
section: From Lesson 4.2: Where Bias Comes From
text:
From Lesson 4.2: Where Bias Comes From

Gender Shades: Who Is Missing from the Data

Joy Buolamwini, a researcher at MIT, and Timnit Gebru tested face programs from big companies. The programs had to say if a face was a man or a woman.

For lighter-skinned men, they were wrong less than 1% of the time.
For darker-skinned women, they were wrong up to 35% of the time.

Why? The training photos had far more lighter-skinned faces. The programs had less practice with everyone else. After her study, the companies improved their programs.

An AI is only as good as its training examples. People who are missing from the data get worse results.


More AI Shortcuts
The wolf AI from the lesson was made on purpose, to test people. Other shortcuts were found by surprise.

Horses and a line of text (2019). Researchers studied an AI that sorted photos. It seemed very good at finding horses. But many horse photos in its training data had a small line of text in the corner. It named who owned the photo. The AI learned to look for the text, not the horse.
Chest X-rays (2018). An AI looked for a lung sickness in chest X-rays. Researchers found it could also tell which hospital an X-ray came from, from small marks on the picture. One hospital had many more sick patients. So knowing the hospital could help the AI guess, without looking closely at the lungs.



How Researchers Find Shortcuts

Test with new data from a new place. A husky in snow. X-rays from a different hospital. If the score drops, the AI may be using a shortcut.
Ask the AI where it looked. Some tools color the parts of a picture that the AI used most. For the wolf AI, the tool colored the snow.
crumbs: Explore More: When AI Gets It Wrong

title: Explore More: When AI Gets It Wrong
text:
From Lesson 4.3: Real or Fake?

How AI Learns to Make Faces
One way is a game between two neural networks:





The maker makes fake faces. The checker tries to tell them from real photos. Each time the checker catches a fake, the maker changes its weights. After millions of rounds, the checker can’t tell anymore. Often, neither can we.
Today many tools use diffusion instead (Lesson 3.7). The result is the same: pictures that look real.


Can People Tell?

Scientists Sophie Nightingale and Hany Farid showed people real faces and AI faces.

People were right 48% of the time. That’s the same as guessing.
After a short lesson on clues, people were right 59% of the time.
People rated the AI faces as a little more trustworthy than the real ones.



Scientists in Australia tested 125 people. 36 of them were super-recognizers: people with an amazing memory for faces.

The scientists took out every AI face with an easy clue, like strange teeth or ears.
Most people did only a little better than guessing. Super-recognizers did only a little better than that.
People felt sure they could spot the AI faces, even when they couldn’t.
The best AI faces gave themselves away by being too perfect: very average, with both sides almost the same. That clue may not last either.




Labels That Show Where a Picture Came From

Some cameras and AI tools now add Content Credentials: hidden information that says how a picture was made. Some websites show a small “CR” label you can click. Most pictures online still don’t have this information, and it can be removed.



“That Is AI!”
When fakes are everywhere, there’s a second problem. A person caught on a real video can say, “That is fake. It was made with AI.” Some people will believe them.
In 2018, two law professors, Bobby Chesney and Danielle Citron, gave this problem a name: the liar’s dividend. A dividend is a reward. Fakes give liars a reward: an easy way to deny the truth. This is one more reason to check the source, not just the picture.
crumbs: Explore More: When AI Gets It Wrong

title: Explore More: When AI Gets It Wrong
section: From Lesson 4.4: Why AI Cheat Detectors Fail
text:
From Lesson 4.4: Why AI Cheat Detectors Fail

Even Its Makers Gave Up

In 2023, OpenAI, the company that makes ChatGPT, made its own detector. It found only 26% of AI writing. It called 9% of human writing “AI.” OpenAI shut it down after 6 months because it wasn’t accurate enough.



How Real Detectors Measure Words
Imagine a chatbot reading your essay one word at a time. Before each word, it guesses what comes next. If it guesses right most of the time, your writing is predictable. Many detectors work this way.
Some detectors also look at sentence length. People often mix long sentences and short ones. AI writing often keeps them about the same. But many careful writers, and many English learners, also write sentences of about the same length.


The Stanford Study, in More Detail
The researchers tested 7 detectors on 91 essays by people learning English.

On average, the detectors called 61% of the essays “AI.”
Almost all of them (98%) were called “AI” by at least one detector.
All 7 detectors agreed on about 1 in 5 essays. All 7 were wrong.

Then the researchers asked ChatGPT to rewrite the same essays with fancier words. The detectors called far fewer of them “AI.” The writing became more AI, and the detectors said it was less AI.

title: Explore More: AI in the Real World
text:
From Lesson 5.1: Your Data, Your Privacy
This page goes with Unit 5. Read it on your own, if you want to learn more. Nothing here is homework. Each section goes with one lesson.
crumbs: Explore More: AI in the Real World

title: Explore More: AI in the Real World
text:
Data Brokers
A data broker is a company that collects information about people and sells it. It buys data from apps, stores, and websites. It puts the pieces together into a file about one person: where they live, what they buy, where they go.
You never signed up with a data broker. Most people don’t even know their names. Some states now have laws that let you ask a data broker to delete your file.


Searching by Face
Some companies collected billions of photos from the internet: from news sites, school pages, and social media. They used AI to make a face search. You give it one photo of a person, and it finds other photos of the same person online, with their name.
Some police departments have used these tools. People disagree about them. Supporters say they help catch criminals. Critics say people never agreed to have their faces used, and that face programs make more mistakes on some faces (Lesson 4.2).


What Happens to Your Chats?
When you type into a chatbot, your words go to the company’s computers. Some companies use chats to train their next AI, unless you turn that off. School AI tools have their own rules.

AI companies keep changing their rules about chats. Ask your teacher what our class AI tool does with what you type. The safest rule doesn’t change: never type anything personal.
crumbs: Explore More: AI in the Real World

title: Explore More: AI in the Real World
text:
From Lesson 5.2: AI Scams

The Scams That Cost the Most
The biggest losses often start with a friendly message from a stranger: “Sorry, wrong number!” The stranger becomes a friend over weeks. Then they share a “great investment,” often in crypto. The website shows your money growing. It’s fake. When you try to take the money out, it’s gone.
Warning signs: a stranger who becomes a close friend fast, never meets you in person or on video, and talks about money.


A Voice-Clone Call
In 2023, a mother in Arizona got a phone call. She heard her 15-year-old daughter crying for help. A man said he had kidnapped her and wanted money. The voice sounded exactly like her daughter.
Her daughter was safe the whole time, at a sports practice. The voice was made with AI. The mother later told her story to the U.S. Senate. This is why a family safe word (Lesson 4.3) matters.


How to Report a Scam

Tell a trusted adult first.
In the United States, you can report scams to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. It works in English and Spanish.
Don’t feel ashamed. Scams fool smart people every day. Reporting helps stop the scammer.
crumbs: Explore More: AI in the Real World

title: Explore More: AI in the Real World
text:
From Lesson 5.3: AI and Jobs

The ATM Story
ATMs made each bank branch cheaper to run. So banks opened more branches, and each one needed fewer tellers. For about 30 years, the total number of tellers in the United States stayed about the same, or grew a little. Tellers did less counting and more helping customers.
Later, people started banking on their phones. Then teller jobs did go down. The same machine can help jobs at first and cut them later.


Machines That Changed Work Before

Tractors. In 1900, about 4 in 10 workers in the United States worked on farms. Today it’s fewer than 2 in 100. Farms grow more food than ever.
Spreadsheets. Programs like Excel do in seconds the math that clerks did by hand. Jobs that only added up numbers went away. Jobs that used the numbers to make decisions grew.

Some people say AI is the same story again: some jobs shrink, new jobs grow. Others say AI is different, because it can do thinking work, not just hand work. Nobody knows for sure yet.


The Jobs Studies

Stanford (August 2025): Erik Brynjolfsson and other researchers looked at millions of paychecks. In the jobs most exposed to AI, like software and customer service, workers aged 22 to 25 had about 13% fewer jobs than expected. Older workers in the same jobs did fine. One idea: AI does many of the tasks that beginners used to learn on.
Yale (October 2025): Researchers looked at the whole job market since ChatGPT came out. They didn’t find a big change yet.

section: From Lesson 5.4: AI and the News
text:
From Lesson 5.4: AI and the News

“People Like You”
A feed doesn’t learn only from you. It also learns from people like you. If many people who watched the same 5 videos as you then watched a sixth video, the app guesses you’ll like it too. This is called a recommendation system. It’s a kind of machine learning.


News Websites Written by AI
Some websites look like local newspapers. They have a name, a logo, and new stories every hour. But no reporters work there. AI writes the stories, often by rewriting other news. Some of it’s wrong. The sites make money from ads.
How to check: Is there a list of real reporters with real names? Does the site have a phone number and an address? Do other news sites ever mention it?


A Fake Voice in an Election
In January 2024, many voters in New Hampshire got a phone call. It sounded like President Joe Biden. The voice told them not to vote in the state’s primary election. The voice was made with AI.
The man who made the calls was fined 6 million dollars by the Federal Communications Commission. Since then, many states have passed laws about AI in election ads.

title: Explore More: AI and Our Future
text:
The Art Contest Story
Jason Allen’s winning picture was called Théâtre D’opéra Spatial (French for “Space Opera Theater”). He said he spent more than 80 hours on it and made hundreds of versions before he chose one. Then he changed it with other software.
He asked the U.S. Copyright Office to register it as his work. In 2023, the office said no: most of the picture was made by the AI, not by him. Allen went to court. People still argue: are hundreds of prompts and choices enough to make a person the artist?


The Court Cases
Artists, writers, news companies, and music companies have taken AI companies to court. Their main question: is it fair to train an AI on someone’s work without asking them or paying them?
AI companies say training is like a student who reads many books and then writes something new. Artists say a student doesn’t copy millions of works in a few weeks, and doesn’t compete with every artist at once. Courts in different countries may answer differently.


AI Music
AI can now make songs, with singing, from a short prompt. Some AI songs have sounded so much like real singers that music companies asked websites to take them down. Many musicians use AI as a tool: to try ideas, clean up recordings, or translate a song into another language. Others refuse to use it at all.

title: Explore More: AI and Our Future
text:
From Lesson 6.2: AI Friends

What Research Says
In 2025, researchers at MIT and OpenAI studied people who talked with a chatbot every day for a month. On average, the people who used it the most felt more lonely at the end, and spent less time with other people. The study can’t show what caused what. Maybe lonely people talk to chatbots more. But it’s a warning sign.
Other studies found that a short chat helped some people feel a little better for a while. The difference may be how much, and what the chat replaces. A chat that helps you practice talking to people is different from a chat that replaces them.


Why It Feels Real
Remember the ELIZA effect (Lesson 1.3): people feel understood by a computer, even when they know it’s a program. Modern chatbots are trained on millions of real conversations. They know what a caring friend would say next. Saying the right words isn’t the same as caring. But it can feel the same.

title: Explore More: AI and Our Future
text:
From Lesson 6.3: The Hidden Costs

Training Costs Too
Before a chatbot answers anyone, it is trained. Training a big model uses thousands of special computer chips for weeks or months. That uses a lot of electricity. For the biggest models, estimates say it’s about as much as hundreds or thousands of homes use in a year. Then the model answers billions of questions, and those answers add up too.


Your Brain Runs on 20 Watts
Your brain uses about 20 watts: less than many light bulbs. With that, it sees, talks, walks, feels, and learns from a few examples. Scientists are studying the brain to find ways to make AI use less energy.


The Data Labelers’ Story
In 2023, TIME magazine reported on workers in Kenya who labeled data for OpenAI through another company. They read descriptions of violence and abuse all day, so the AI could learn to refuse to repeat them. They were paid less than $2 an hour. Some said the work hurt their mental health. After the story, workers in Kenya started organizing to ask for better pay and support.
Data labeling is real work that makes AI safer and smarter. Many people say the workers deserve fair pay and protection.

section: From Lesson 6.4: Who Makes the Rules?
text:
From Lesson 6.4: Who Makes the Rules?

More Trolley Problems

The footbridge: you stand on a bridge above the track, next to a large person. If you push them off, they’ll stop the trolley and save 5 people. Most people say no, even though the numbers are the same as pulling the lever. Why does pushing feel different?
The doctor: a doctor could save 5 sick patients by taking organs from 1 healthy visitor. Almost everyone says this is wrong. What makes it different from the lever?

Philosophers use these stories to find the rules people really use: not just counting lives, but also what you do with your own hands, and people’s rights.


The Moral Machine Results
The Moral Machine study was published in 2018. It found three choices that most people in most places made. Save people over animals. Save more lives over fewer. Save young people over old. But the strength of each choice was different in different parts of the world. Some people asked: should a car’s choices depend on which country it drives in?


How a Law Is Made
In the United States, a law can come from Congress (for the whole country) or from a state. People can tell lawmakers what they think by writing, calling, or speaking at public meetings. Students can do this too. Many AI laws started because someone told their story to lawmakers.

title: Explore More: AI and Our Future
text:
From Lesson 6.5: Possible Futures

The Experts’ Debate
In 2023, hundreds of AI scientists and company leaders signed a one-sentence statement. It said that reducing the risk that AI could wipe out humanity should be a global priority, like pandemics and nuclear war. Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, two of the “godfathers” of neural networks, signed it.
Other experts disagreed strongly. Some, like Yann LeCun, said today’s AI is far from that kind of danger. Others said the statement takes attention away from harms happening now: bias, scams, fakes, and jobs. Many researchers think both kinds of problems matter.


More Alignment Stories
These really happened, with small AIs in research labs:

An AI in a boat racing game was supposed to win the race. It found it could score more points by driving in circles, hitting the same targets again and again, and never finishing.
An AI was supposed to learn to walk in a computer world. It found a mistake in the world’s physics and moved by sliding on the ground instead.

Each AI did exactly what its goal said. Not what people meant. That’s the paper clip problem, in a tiny form.


AI and Medicine
In 2024, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold, an AI that predicts the shape of proteins. Proteins are the tiny machines inside every living thing. Knowing their shapes helps scientists understand diseases and design medicines. Scientists around the world have used AlphaFold’s predictions for hundreds of millions of proteins.
